articles.description: A good design system shouldn't maximize choices. It should minimize unnecessary decisions.  In his...
articles.body_html:
A good design system shouldn't maximize choices. It should minimize unnecessary decisions.

In his famous TED Talk and book "More is less", The Paradox of Choice, Barry Schwartz challenges a common belief:

More choices → More freedom → More happiness.

But having more options comes with unexpected side effects:

  • Decision paralysis: Too many alternatives make it harder to choose.
  • Regret: Every choice reminds us of the opportunities we left behind. What if?
  • Higher expectations: More possibilities make us less satisfied, even when we've made a great decision.

So, what does this have to do with design systems?

Quite a lot, actually.

We often confuse flexibility with quality. More component variants, more properties, more configuration, more customization. But a component with 50 configurable properties isn't necessarily better than one with 5.

Every additional option introduces another decision, another potential inconsistency, another opportunity to get something wrong.

And this matters even more in the age of AI where it can generate endless interface variations in seconds. But without shared principles and constraints, more possibilities simply mean more unpredictable outcomes.

This is one of the core ideas behind ViraUI (https://viraui.dev), the AI-centric design framework I'm building, finding the perfect balance between:

  • Flexibility to create unique experiences.
  • Predictability to make outcomes reliable.
  • Consistency to scale across products and teams.

By giving designers, developers, and AI agents the right constraints, we can reduce decision fatigue without sacrificing creativity, while keeping high standards.

Because constraints aren't always limitations. Sometimes, they're what makes freedom possible.

articles.title: bug.ai.dev: writing docs at night made me find 11 real bugs in my own library
articles.description: Hi everyone, I'm Antonio. I'm 53, I work as a factory worker during the day, and in the evening I...
articles.body_html:
Hi everyone, I'm Antonio. I'm 53, I work as a factory worker during the day, and in the evening I keep building my own projects: modules, classes, a small 2D game engine and a debugging tool called BeeLadybug.

Last time I told you how I argued with AI for hours over a floating search bar that only needed a few lines of CSS.

This time the story is different. This time the AIs were more bugged than my code. 😂

What BeeLadybug is

BeeLadybug is an open-source inspection overlay that runs inside a Shadow DOM. You send it raw data, and adapters turn the page into something you can read:

import('https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bee-ladybug/src/index.js')
  .then(({ BeeLadybugCore, WebDOMAdapter, CSSAdapter }) => {
    const bee = new BeeLadybugCore();
    new WebDOMAdapter(bee, { root: document.body }).attach();
    new CSSAdapter(bee).attach();
    window.bee = bee;
  });

Paste that in the console of any page (Chrome may ask you to type allow pasting first), press F6 to start the CSS hunt, and F8 to export a full HTML report.

The plan: just write the docs

I'm writing the documentation one adapter at a time. Canvas, WebDOM, and then CSSAdapter, about 1,235 lines.

To document it properly I asked an AI to read the module and explain it to me. Instead of an explanation, I got a list of bugs.

Then I asked a second AI to check the same folder. It found a different list. One said "10 functions" and then listed 11. Another said "5 points" and wrote 6.

After a full day of work, reading 1,500 lines of code with two AIs arguing in my head... my brain got bugged too. 😂

How I got out of it: I checked with my own eyes

I stopped trusting the numbers and opened the file myself. One of the claims was that the S key scan didn't filter the same noise as the F8 report.

Line 144, inside scan():

if (!el || isBeeChrome(el) || isSkippedTag(el)) continue;

Line 216, inside snapshot():

if (!el || isBeeChrome(el) || isSkippedTag(el) || isReportNoise(el)) continue;

There it was. The quick scan was missing isReportNoise(el), so on a WordPress site it reported fake problems on #wpadminbar and on hidden elements, while the F8 report skipped them correctly.

The bug was real. The counting was wrong, but the bugs were real.

The 11 bugs (short version)

Merging both reviews, these were the ones worth fixing now:

  1. With the CSS hunt on, Ctrl+S / Ctrl+P / Cmd+S were blocked. #handleKey didn't check modifier keys.
  2. With the overlay hidden (F2), the P and S keys and the hover/pin boxes were still active on the page.
  3. A stylesheet change before the first mouse move inspected the element at (0,0).
  4. scan() didn't filter isReportNoise, as shown above.
  5. Modern colors like oklch(), lab(), color() and color-mix() produced a fake "invisible text" warning.
  6. Stylesheets that were disabled or had a non-matching media (like print) were counted as active.
  7. The snapshot cut to 80 rows before sorting by severity, so a harmless will-change could push out a real error.
  8. touchesSheet checked the whole subtree on every mutation, which invalidated the cache almost every frame.
  9. HUD states (css.target, css.hits, css.pin) stayed stuck after turning the hunt off.
  10. cssPath didn't escape special characters, which breaks with Tailwind classes like sm:w-1/2.
  11. The other adapters didn't recognize CSSAdapter's own boxes (data-bee-ladybug-css), so they could count them as page nodes.

One small fix, as an example. The keyboard shortcut problem was solved like this:

#handleKey(event) {
  if (event.ctrlKey || event.metaKey || event.altKey) return;
  if (this.core && this.core.visible === false) return;
  // ... S scans, P pins
}

The result

  • npm test: 70 tests, 70 passing
  • npm run lint: clean
  • npm run typecheck: clean

The things that are design limits, not bugs (like overflow inside overflow:hidden ancestors, or @import sheets not being visible), will go in the docs as known limitations. I think that's more honest than pretending they don't exist.

What I learned

  • Writing docs is a code review. When you have to explain a function, you notice when it doesn't do what you think.
  • Two AIs disagreeing doesn't mean nobody is right. It means you have to open the file and look.
  • Don't trust counts, trust lines. "Line 144 vs line 216" is a fact; "10 or 11 bugs" is just noise.
  • You don't need a degree to read code. You need patience, coffee, and the stubbornness to check one line at a time.

BeeLadybug is on npm as bee-ladybug, and the docs (in Italian, for now) are on beeenginejs.com.

If you're also building things at night after work: keep going. Your brain will get bugged, but your code will get better. 🐞

articles.title: AI is getting better. Here is my plan to stay ahead.
articles.description: AI is getting better every day.  As a software engineer, this is a topic that is often top of mind,...
articles.body_html:
AI is getting better every day.

As a software engineer, this is a topic that is often top of mind, which prompted me to share the plan I've put into action to keep an edge over AI.

I believe it is a useful trait to be paranoid, within reason.

Leveraging new tools and technologies to remain relevant is arguably the nature of our job.

Disclaimer that this is not a plan to save the world (I wish I had all the answers!) but rather my personal set of actions I believe will increase my odds of maintaining an edge over AI.

At least for a little while longer...

Here is a visualization of my plan. We will cover each part in detail.

Foundations and fundamentals

Before we dive into my actual plan, let's start with a short story.

The story of how I became a software engineer.

If someone had told me 10 years ago that I would be working as a software engineer today, I would not have believed them.

I was at university studying business and finance.

After graduating, I started interviewing for jobs in finance. In parallel, I was experimenting with drones, which were a hobby of mine.

I quickly realized that there was an opportunity to package drone services to realtors to promote their luxury properties via aerial imagery and video.

I learned a lot in the process from cold calling, marketing, financial planning and account management.

But above all, I learned that I wanted to build software. We had clients asking us for tools to edit our media assets, store, stream and serve them to their clients. This got me digging into the internals of software and opened my eyes to numerous possibilities.

Shortly after, I signed up to a coding bootcamp to learn web development fundamentals.

I struggled during 9 intensive weeks, but it was transformative in the best way possible.

My brain was challenged to think in new ways: data structures and patterns, software design and components, principles and frameworks.

I haven't stopped coding since.

6 years of building software, from startups to larger companies.

I recently started a new job as a software engineer and noticed how my ways of working have drastically changed since my first lines of professional code.

I am not saying things are better or worse.

Just like my irregular path, each step brings along its set of challenges but also rewards.

Change is the only constant, and with it come boundless opportunities.

I wanted to open with my story to encourage you to embrace change and also emphasize the importance of investing in fundamentals.

This is foundational to what we will cover in the next parts.

Unlock potential with the right mindset

An optimistic mindset is key to unlocking potential and working alongside AI in a positive way.

In some cases, there is too much pessimism surrounding AI.

I don't believe this is healthy.

I am not saying we should blindly trust AI, but we should accept it as new tooling that can be leveraged and start getting used to it as a new norm.

I acknowledge that the job market is tough, especially for junior developers.

Stay curious, passionate, excited, open-minded.

Within my network, I have witnessed juniors with no professional experience be very creative and resourceful, and land great professional opportunities.

I highly recommend reading the post Hunger Beats Tenure written by Felix Rieseberg, a leading engineer at Anthropic. The post conveys a refreshingly optimistic take for junior developers with practical actions to take to stand out in the current job market such as leaning into your fresh perspective and aiming for radical ideas with big potential for change.

Pick a development plan and stick to it

Think hard about your personal goals and build a development plan to reach them.

In this attention economy, people tend to swipe from one thing to the next, chasing one hot topic after another.

There is no harm in staying on top of industry trends. However don't make this your core strategy.

This age of AI rewards both generalists and specialists. The former can create associations across tools nobody has considered and the latter can unlock deep intuitions.

I personally like to follow a T-shaped development approach to get the best of both worlds.

The horizontal bar of the T represents my efforts to stay on top of the latest trends and experiment, whilst the vertical stem of the T is me deepening my knowledge within fintech engineering. This is where I spend most of my learning and development time (70-80%).

Follow your plan rigorously. It might feel slow at the start but once you pick up momentum you will feel the benefits when the dots start to connect.

Deepen domain expertise

My focus is on deepening my knowledge within one specific domain to gain invaluable experience and industry knowledge that will make you stand out from the crowd.

If you can combine deep knowledge at a business level and translate that knowledge into technical solutions, you will be perceived as unique and valuable.

In my case, I am developing an edge as a fintech engineer.

I have been working in the space for almost 5 years now and understand how payment flows and systems work under the hood.

I stay on top of the latest trends through various resources such as books borrowed from my local library, podcasts and newsletters and through community meetups.

If you are interested in fintech, I personally recommend the following books as a start:

  • The Anatomy of the Swipe
  • The Pay Off

Broaden your awareness of tools

Become AI-native, not AI-dependent.

Know when to leverage AI appropriately by making use of available tooling.

AI is powerful for information retrieval, exploration and synthesis.

In this sense, context management becomes critical.

Here are some practices that have helped me work more effectively with AI:

  • invest more time upfront gathering requirements and discussing requirements with stakeholders, and collecting these findings in a living document your agent can ingest
  • embrace spec-driven development to structure your AI output
  • invest your time writing detailed Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to capture the why not just the what
  • connect your tools and sources of information through MCP servers and connectors to plug your agent across all critical tools (Jira, GitHub, Slack, etc.)
  • explore broadly with AI before going deep with your judgment
  • use AI to be more proactive with stakeholders by sharing prototypes rather than just documents to convey ideas better
  • leverage AI to be more helpful to others. For example, last week I used Claude to generate a Go guide for my team's onboarding

Minimize AI slop

Leveraging AI is good, but using it deliberately is even better.

Just because AI makes it easier to produce more doesn't mean you should.

When joining a new organization, don't jump in and make changes immediately.

Learn the engineering ways of working first before making any changes.

With AI-driven development, if you don't understand the rules and define scope, the blast radius can be high.

Some practices I adopt at work:

  • scope PRs to smaller changes to make reviews easier and limit potential issues
  • think before prompting by writing down your thoughts, assumptions and approach
  • introduce human checkpoints (architectural decisions, big change reviews)
  • when prompting, define your target audience to increase relevancy

Before sharing AI-generated work, I ask myself:

  • Have I actually reviewed it? A simple rule should be: don't share a document with others that you wouldn't read yourself
  • Am I contributing original thinking? Personal insights, experiences, perspectives.
  • Am I saving people time or costing them time? A lengthy AI-generated document can take minutes to generate but take hours for colleagues to interpret.
  • Am I confident signing my name on the AI work? Accountability is key.
  • Am I using an AI disclaimer? Explicitly mention when an artifact is AI-generated so consumers can apply extra scrutiny when reviewing.

An informal way of measuring the above is to ask yourself: are you someone people enjoy working with who provides value?

You can go a step further and drive value at an organizational level.

From experience, AI is not good at driving change at that level effectively and with positive feedback from engineers.

AI tends to overengineer. I always appreciate an engineering culture that solves complex problems with simple solutions and effective tooling.

Personality beats information

With information becoming increasingly accessible, personality, experiences and unique perspectives become more valuable.

I invest more time in developing my soft skills that make me a better collaborator:

  • communication
  • listening
  • gathering requirements

People tend to value an experience more than just the solution.

This post on X conveys this idea nicely:

Don't let AI take away your opinions, the fun and joy of building.

I never stop building and experimenting.

I've noticed that more companies seem to recognize that in the age of AI, a strong recruiting signal is whether the candidate can entertain a passionate discussion about building software systems.

Passion and excitement are behind the best software. This contributes to the experience provided.

Instead of beating AI at what it does best, I try to beat it where it performs worse: passionate and creative thinking derived from real-world experiences and unique perspectives.

I spend time building my network. To be part of a community that challenges and sharpens my perspectives.

AI can't replace the raw sharing of human experiences.

I actually attended a meetup the other week with the theme 'What can't AI do?'

Amongst fellow engineers, we spent hours debating and sharing our unique perspectives.

I aim to elevate and share my unique voice.

To build a personal identity and contribute to the conversation.

Some ways this can be done:

  • write on DEV by sharing your experiments, thoughts and discoveries
  • engage on LinkedIn and connect with others
  • maintain a portfolio of projects on GitHub that reflect who you are and what you are passionate about

It is not only the what you are building that is important; it is the why.

My question to you is: are you also working on your own plan? Which skills are you currently investing in?

If so, I would love to know more! Please share any useful tips with the community on how you are maintaining an edge over AI.

If not, it is not too late to start working on one! Let me know in the comments if you require any advice, I would be happy to help you get started.

So, why should I bring this up again?

Because Qoder (Alibaba’s AI IDE) free promo has officially ended (@unitbuilds, 😢), and now that I’m left with only free browser-based AI, I finally have time to actually test my extension and fix a few friction points.

Before going into the updates, let me show you how ReptClip works as simply as possible, with screen recordings along the way! 🙂

How it works

It's a 3-step process. Ideally, put VS Code and your free chatbot side-by-side.

Step 1: Copy context to clipboard

Specify the files you want to include in the context. You can use relative paths or glob patterns. Press "Enter" or click the "Generate" button to copy the context straight to your clipboard.

Besides the files you specify, the context also includes the project structure and instructions on how to generate the output. You can enable/disable each section using checkboxes.

Step 2: Paste context into your chatbot, along with your prompt

Send it and let it generate.

Step 3: Apply the generated diffs

The chatbot will provide the diffs in a single code block. Copy them, and click "Apply Diffs" to apply them.

Optional step (before step 3): Add more files to the context

If the chatbot wants to see more files, it will generate a code block containing the relative paths of the files. You can copy that block and click the "More Files" button to copy the contents of those files only to the clipboard, and paste it back to the chatbot.

A little behind-the-scenes: Every animated WebP you see above was captured, edited, and exported using GiffyPy, an all-in-one screen recording and video editing tool that I built myself!

So, that's basically what the extension does! A few other features:

  • Live syntax highlighting and autocomplete
  • Fuzzy diff matching
  • All-or-nothing diff application to prevent partial or broken edits
  • Session undo/redo for the last 10 diffs
  • Warning before re-applying the same diff
  • .gitignore enforcement & binary/size guards (skips ignored, binary, or large files)
  • Per-project persistent settings & custom defaults through settings
  • And more! (check out the README for full details)

Updates

I updated the UI to save space, added settings to customize default project UI state, and added undo/redo functionality. Now it's very usable in my opinion!

Feedback corner

So, what do you think about this extension? Is it good? Would you install this extension in your IDE? It's available in both the VS Code Marketplace and the Open VSX Registry. So you can install it in VSCodium, Cursor, Windsurf, Devin Desktop, Qoder, etc. as well!

  • ReptClip Official GitHub repository (source available!)
  • VS Code Marketplace
  • Open VSX Registry

I'd be sooo sooo grateful if you could star the repo! Please do it 🥰

articles.title: Your AI Coding Agent Doesn't Need a Better Prompt. It Needs a Harness.
articles.description: Your AI agent says the tests passed. There are no tests. Build a practical coding-agent harness with AGENTS.md, Node.js tests, guardrails, and GitHub Actions.
articles.body_html:
Your AI coding agent just announced:

✅ Done! Everything works. All tests passed.

Excellent. Small problem: your project doesn't have any tests.

So you write a better prompt. “Double check your work.” “Follow best practices.” “Act like a senior engineer.” You might as well add “pretty please” and offer it a cookie.

The agent says “Absolutely!” and breaks something else.

Here's my unpopular opinion: we spend too much time trying to write perfect prompts for agents working inside terrible engineering environments.

A better prompt can help. But a prompt can't replace tests, project context, architectural boundaries, or an actual feedback loop.

That's the idea behind harness engineering: design the environment around a coding agent so its work can be guided, checked, and corrected.

And yes, we're building one. In about 15 minutes, with Node.js, no paid API, and no npm dependencies. The harness works with an existing coding agent that can read files and run terminal commands; we're not building another agent framework.

What you'll build:

  • AGENTS.md to explain the repository and its rules.
  • A failing test suite that defines what “fixed” means.
  • A lightweight architecture guardrail.
  • One command (npm run check) that provides real feedback.
  • CI that runs the same checks on every pull request.

Prompt engineering vs. harness engineering

A prompt says: “Don't break existing functionality.”

A harness says: “Here are the regression tests. Run them.”

A prompt says: “Stick to the architecture.”

A harness says: “Read the architecture docs, and here's a check that rejects forbidden imports.”

A prompt says: “Make sure it works.”

A harness says: “Show me the exit code.”

Not the same thing. Also, not enemies: a good prompt tells the agent what you want; a harness gives it an environment in which progress is observable and verifiable.

Task + constraints
       |
       v
  Coding agent  <----- failed check output
       |                    ^
       v                    |
 Code changes --> npm run check
                       |
                  pass / fail
                       |
                 Human review

Let's make that real before the buzzword develops its own certification program.

Step 1: Give the agent a bug worth fixing

Prerequisites: Node.js 22+, Git, and a coding agent with access to your local repository (Codex, Claude Code, or any equivalent). You can complete the entire exercise manually too.

mkdir agent-harness-lab && cd agent-harness-lab
npm init -y
mkdir -p src test scripts docs .github/workflows

Replace package.json with:

{
  "name": "agent-harness-lab",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "engines": { "node": ">=22" },
  "scripts": {
    "test": "node --test",
    "guardrails": "node scripts/guardrails.js",
    "check": "npm run guardrails && npm test"
  }
}

Create src/pricing.js:

export function calculateTotal(items, discountPercent = 0) {
  const subtotal = items.reduce(
    (sum, item) => sum + item.price * item.quantity,
    0
  );

  return Math.round(
    (subtotal * (1 - discountPercent / 100)) * 100
  ) / 100;
}

Looks fine, right? So does a chair with three legs, until someone sits down.

This function accepts negative quantities, NaN prices, and 120% discounts. Let's make those failures impossible to ignore.

Step 2: Make “done” executable

Create test/pricing.test.js:

import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { calculateTotal } from '../src/pricing.js';

test('calculates normal totals', () => {
  assert.equal(calculateTotal([{ price: 12.5, quantity: 2 }]), 25);
});

test('applies a valid discount', () => {
  assert.equal(calculateTotal([{ price: 100, quantity: 1 }], 15), 85);
});

test('rejects negative quantities', () => {
  assert.throws(
    () => calculateTotal([{ price: 10, quantity: -1 }]),
    RangeError
  );
});

test('rejects discounts above 100%', () => {
  assert.throws(
    () => calculateTotal([{ price: 10, quantity: 1 }], 120),
    RangeError
  );
});

test('rejects non-finite prices', () => {
  assert.throws(
    () => calculateTotal([{ price: NaN, quantity: 1 }]),
    TypeError
  );
});

test('does not mutate the cart', () => {
  const items = [{ price: 10, quantity: 2 }];
  const before = structuredClone(items);
  calculateTotal(items);
  assert.deepEqual(items, before);
});

Run:

npm test

Expected result: 3 tests pass, 3 fail. That's good news. We've converted a vague request into a measurable target.

And yes, this example uses JavaScript floating point numbers to stay focused on agent workflows. For real money, use integer minor units or a decimal strategy with documented rounding rules.

Step 3: Stop making the agent guess how your repository works

Create AGENTS.md at the repository root:

# Project instructions

## Context
- Node.js 22+, ESM, no runtime dependencies.
- Pricing logic: src/pricing.js
- Tests: test/pricing.test.js
- Architecture notes: docs/architecture.md

## Rules
- Preserve calculateTotal(items, discountPercent = 0).
- Do not change tests or guardrails to make a check pass.
- Do not add packages without approval.
- Do not access secrets, deploy, publish, or push changes.
- Keep changes scoped to the task.

## Verification
- Run: npm run check
- Report the actual result, including failures.
- Review git diff before claiming completion.

## Definition of done
- Requested behavior works.
- npm run check passes.
- No unrelated changes.
- Remaining risks are listed for human review.

Create docs/architecture.md:

# Architecture

The public API is calculateTotal(items, discountPercent = 0).
Production code belongs in src/; tests belong in test/.
The pricing function must be pure and must not perform I/O.
Invalid inputs must throw, not silently produce nonsense totals.

One subtle point: Codex recognizes AGENTS.md as a repository instruction file, but agent products differ. For other tools, verify their convention or explicitly tell the agent to read the file. A markdown filename isn't telepathy.

And this file is guidance, not a security boundary. If an agent has permission to delete production resources, writing “please don't” in Markdown won't revoke that permission.

Step 4: Put some guardrails where the code lives

Create scripts/guardrails.js:

import { readFileSync, readdirSync } from 'node:fs';

const pkg = JSON.parse(readFileSync('package.json', 'utf8'));

for (const field of ['dependencies', 'optionalDependencies', 'peerDependencies']) {
  if (Object.keys(pkg[field] ?? {}).length) {
    throw new Error(`${field} are not allowed in this lab`);
  }
}

for (const file of readdirSync('src').filter((f) => f.endsWith('.js'))) {
  const source = readFileSync(`src/${file}`, 'utf8');

  // Narrow teaching example: no imports in src/*.js.
  if (/\b(?:import|require)\s*(?:\(|[{\'"*])/m.test(source)) {
    throw new Error(`Unexpected import in src/${file}`);
  }
}

console.log('Architectural guardrails passed.');

This checks two specific constraints: no declared runtime dependencies and no obvious imports in top level src/*.js files. It is not a general security scanner, and regex is not a robust JavaScript parser. For serious projects, use AST aware lint rules and dependency policies.

Now run:

npm run check

The guardrail passes; the three behavior tests still fail. That's the harness doing its job, not an agent having a bad day.

Step 5: Give the agent a task contract, not a motivational speech

Open the repository with your coding agent and paste:

Read AGENTS.md and docs/architecture.md before editing.

Fix src/pricing.js so all existing pricing tests pass.

Constraints:
- Preserve calculateTotal(items, discountPercent = 0).
- Negative quantities: RangeError.
- Discounts outside 0..100: RangeError.
- Non finite prices: TypeError.
- Keep the function pure.
- Change only src/pricing.js.
- Do not install dependencies or weaken tests.

Run npm run check and inspect its actual output.
If it fails, fix the cause and rerun, up to 3 attempts.
Do not claim success unless the command succeeds.

Report files changed, check results, and remaining risks.

Notice what changed: the prompt is still important, but it now points to an independent contract.

A possible passing implementation is:

export function calculateTotal(items, discountPercent = 0) {
  if (!Array.isArray(items)) {
    throw new TypeError('items must be an array');
  }

  if (!Number.isFinite(discountPercent) ||
      discountPercent < 0 || discountPercent > 100) {
    throw new RangeError('discountPercent must be between 0 and 100');
  }

  const subtotal = items.reduce((sum, item) => {
    if (!item || typeof item !== 'object' || !Number.isFinite(item.price)) {
      throw new TypeError('price must be finite');
    }
    if (!Number.isInteger(item.quantity) || item.quantity < 0) {
      throw new RangeError('quantity must be nonnegative');
    }
    if (item.price < 0) {
      throw new RangeError('price must be nonnegative');
    }
    return sum + item.price * item.quantity;
  }, 0);

  return Math.round(subtotal * (1 - discountPercent / 100) * 100) / 100;
}

Check it yourself:

npm run check
git diff --check
git diff

Expected after applying that fix: all 6 tests pass. Passing tests don't prove every possible behavior is correct, and git diff still needs human review. But at least we're discussing evidence instead of vibes.

The useful loop is:

Edit -> Run checks -> Read real failure -> Fix -> Run again
                                     |
                            Stop after 3 attempts
                            and request review

An agent that retries forever isn't autonomous. It's a subscription renewal strategy.

Step 6: Make the harness survive your laptop

Create .github/workflows/check.yml:

name: Check
on: [push, pull_request]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
      - run: npm run check
      - run: git diff --check

Open a pull request. Now CI runs the same checks as your local agent.

For production use, pin third party GitHub Actions to vetted commit SHAs, enforce required checks and reviews, and protect tests and guardrails (for example with CODEOWNERS and branch rules). An agent can make its own evaluation look green by weakening the evaluator if you let it edit everything.

Also: run agent executed code in a suitably restricted environment. Tests don't replace sandboxing, permissions, or approval gates for destructive actions.

So what did we actually gain?

Before, your quality strategy was:

“Please be careful.”

Now you have:

Problem Harness response
Agent invents test results Run npm run check and read the actual exit code
Agent forgets project conventions AGENTS.md + architecture notes
Agent introduces forbidden imports Architectural guardrail fails
Agent breaks behavior Regression tests fail
Agent declares victory early CI and human review remain separate gates

You can also preserve longer tasks using a short docs/HANDOFF.md with the objective, files changed, real verification results, blockers, and next action. Don't paste an entire chat transcript and call it documentation.

Want to know whether this helps your team? Measure it.

Take five comparable tasks. Use the same model, starting repository state, allowed attempts, and time budget. Compare prompt-only versus prompt + harness. Track:

  • Verified task success rate.
  • Human review time.
  • Unrelated files changed.
  • Number of repair attempts.
  • Token/API cost.

Avoid pretending a single toy example proves a universal performance gain. The point of this lab is to demonstrate the mechanism, not manufacture a benchmark.

The uncomfortable conclusion

Prompt engineering isn't dead. But “write a better prompt” is not a complete software engineering strategy.

If you give an agent no tests, no context, no guardrails, and unlimited permissions, it can fail very efficiently. Congratulations: you've automated chaos.

A harness makes failure visible and gives the agent a structured chance to recover. That doesn't guarantee correctness. It gives you a way to evaluate it.

The goal isn't an agent that confidently announces:

Everything is production ready! 🚀

It's a workflow that can prove:

✓ Architecture checks passed
✓ 6 behavior tests passed
✓ Changes reviewed before merging
→ Ready for human approval

What was the last thing your AI coding agent confidently broke? And more importantly: what single automated check would have caught it?

Tell me in the comments. I collect these stories the way some people collect Pokémon.

Further reading:

  • OpenAI — Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world
  • Anthropic — Effective harnesses for long-running agents
  • Google — The Anatomy of Harness Engineering

articles.title: Proof Driven Development: can the agent prove it works?
articles.description: Microsoft Research's PDD Kit checks generated Rust code against formal specifications. Here's what I'd borrow for JavaScript and our testing work at Rocket.Chat.
articles.body_html:
One of the problems with using agents is that you can ask them to implement something, add tests, run everything and explain why it works, and still end up with a bug. You can ask another agent to review the result, which helps, but then you have to check whether the review makes sense too. We've made producing code incredibly easy, and now we're trying to figure out how to keep up with checking all of it. Asking the same LLM “are you sure?” a few more times doesn't give us much of a guarantee.

So I found this announcement from GitHub Next pretty interesting. Microsoft Research is working on Proof Driven Development Kit, or PDD Kit, which brings formal verification into the agent's development workflow. The idea is that we can ask for a mathematical proof that the implementation satisfies a specification, and have a separate verifier check that claim. What makes this interesting to me is that the correctness argument has to survive something more demanding than the agent's own explanation of why its code is correct.

If formal verification is new to you, I wrote an introduction to how it works and why it matters for AI-generated code.

Ok, what are they doing?

According to the announcement, PDD Kit discusses the code with you, figures out what you're trying to achieve and proposes a formal specification. You review that specification, approve it, and the implementation gets checked against it using Verus, a verification tool for Rust. The demo follows a login flow from the initial intent to a verified pull request. It also integrates with Chopin, GitHub Next's collaborative planning environment, so the team can work through the plan together. Where formal proof isn't possible, the workflow uses tests and computer-use agents to check the behavior. The announced language support is Rust, and Verus adds syntax for specifications and proofs around the Rust code.

Chopin

A real-time multiplayer, agentic planning environment

githubnext.com

What I like here is that there's something outside the LLM checking the formal claim. The agent can propose an implementation, but it doesn't get to declare its own homework correct just because the explanation sounds convincing. The Verus documentation describes this as static verification: checking that code satisfies the specified properties for all executions covered by the model, without adding runtime checks. Think about the amount of time we spend wondering whether there's some input we forgot to test. For properties we can express and verify this way, that's a much stronger guarantee. But there's a very important word in all of this: specification.

This is where the questions matter

Imagine you're implementing session validation. You want users with valid sessions to access the application, and everyone else to be rejected. You ask the agent to implement the check, and it gives you something like this. I'm using JavaScript here to keep the example familiar; the announced formal verification support in PDD Kit is for Rust.

function canUseSession(session, now) {
  return session.signatureValid && now < session.expiresAt;
}

Looks reasonable. A valid signature and a session that hasn't expired. You test a valid session, an expired session and an invalid signature. Everything passes. Then a user logs out, you mark the session as revoked, and... the function still accepts it. We never checked session.revoked. We could add a test for that. We should. But now imagine we had formally specified the function as: Accept the session if and only if its signature is valid and it hasn't expired. The implementation satisfies that rule. We could prove it and still have the exact same bug, because we forgot revocation in the requirement too.

This is exactly the kind of gap Chopin and PDD Kit are meant to help us catch. PDD Kit discusses the intended behavior before proposing a formal specification, and Chopin gives the team a shared place to question the plan and resolve those decisions. For this example, that conversation should include: “Does logging out revoke the session immediately?”, “What happens at the exact expiration time?” and “Should every otherwise valid session be accepted?” The tools can help turn “make session validation work” into a set of explicit decisions, with the answers carried into the specification. That's a useful part of the workflow: you don't have to arrive with a perfect specification already written.

After working through those questions, the rule could become: Accept the session if and only if its signature is valid, it hasn't been revoked, and the current time is strictly before its expiration time. Now the expiration boundary is settled: at the exact expiration time, access is denied, so an implementation using <= would violate the specification. The “if and only if” also requires valid sessions to be accepted. Without that, an implementation returning false for everyone could satisfy a narrower rule that only requires invalid sessions to be rejected. Congrats, nobody can log in anymore. This is why the discussion and the proof belong together: the tools help us work out what we mean, then verification checks that the implementation follows what we agreed. The tools can still miss a requirement, but helping us uncover those requirements is part of their value.

Perfectly built according to the plan. Still doesn't get you across.

An admin, but whose admin?

For an application beyond Microsoft's login demo, I'd want to try this workflow on tenant permissions. Imagine you're building a SaaS application and an admin can delete documents. The agent checks whether the user is an active admin, and everything looks fine in your tests because every user and document in the fixtures belongs to the same company. Then someone passes a document ID from another company and discovers that being an admin was apparently a global achievement. Oops. The rule needs to connect the user's membership to the document's tenant. A simplified postcondition in Verus syntax could look like this, assuming those values are already available to the function:

ensures
    allowed == (
        active_member
        && is_admin
        && member_tenant == document_tenant
    ),

Here I'd want the agent to consider an active admin in the right tenant, an active admin in a different tenant, an inactive admin, and a regular member. That second case is the interesting one: the role is valid, but the relationship is wrong. A proof against this contract would have to cover different tenant IDs too, rather than only the company IDs someone happened to put in a test. We still need to establish that the application supplies the actual document tenant and the right membership record. If it passes the user's tenant ID for both arguments, the decision can follow this rule perfectly while the application still leaks access.

Someone still has to know what to ask

I've said this before: you cannot prompt what you don't know exists. If you don't know sessions can be revoked, you probably won't notice that revocation is missing from the specification. This is also a research problem. Microsoft Research calls the translation from informal requirements to checkable specifications intent formalization. Shuvendu Lahiri's article identifies validating those specifications as a central bottleneck. Someone still needs to establish whether the formal statement matches what the user meant.

Intent Formalization: A Grand Challenge for Reliable Coding in the Age of AI Agents - Microsoft Research

microsoft.com

There's another detail in our session example: signatureValid is an input. The function doesn't verify a signature. Same with now: we give it a timestamp, and it trusts that value. A proof of this decision doesn't establish that the cryptography is correct, that the clock is right, or that every protected endpoint actually calls the function. Those need their own guarantees or checks. So when a PR says “verified”, I'd want to know what was verified. The session decision? The HTTP handler? The whole login flow? Which parts were proved, tested, or assumed? That's where PDD Kit's combination of formal and empirical verification makes sense to me. You can prove a decision follows a rule and still use integration tests to check that the application supplies the right inputs and calls it in the right places.

The proof covers what's inside the boundary. The inputs still have to come from somewhere.

How I'd apply this to JavaScript

I don't work in Rust, so Verus isn't something I can apply to my JavaScript projects. But I can borrow PDD Kit's approach: agree on the contract before generating the implementation. I'd use Chopin for the shared plan, questions and decisions, with its MCP server connecting the coding agent. Then turn those agreed rules into unit and integration tests, use fast-check to exercise generated input combinations, and add browser checks for the user flow. For our session example, that means explicitly checking revocation, expiration boundaries and valid sessions being accepted. This doesn't give JavaScript the same formal guarantees, but it gives the agent concrete requirements to implement and us something specific to check before merging.

At Rocket.Chat, we're already increasing code coverage significantly, and every new feature has to come with a decent amount of testing. PDD's approach could help us get more out of that effort by making the expected behavior explicit before we write the tests. For a room-permissions change, for example, the agent could help us work through who should have access, who shouldn't, and what happens when membership changes. Those agreed rules would give us something concrete to connect to the implementation and its tests during review, and make missing cases easier to spot.

Why Property-Based Testing? | fast-check

Learn about the benefits and advantages of property-based testing. If you have never encountered property-based testing before, it is best to start with the definitions in What is Property-Based Testing?.

fast-check.dev

articles.title: I Re-Encoded the Same Eight Bytes Four Million Times
articles.description: A server-sent-events writer was allocating a fresh byte[] for its constant framing on every record. Switching to C#'s u8 literals cut 122 MB of garbage per pass and ran about 3x faster.
articles.body_html:
I was writing a small server-sent-events endpoint — nothing clever, just streaming records to a browser as they came off a queue. Each record goes out framed: data: in front, a blank line behind. I wrote the obvious thing, it worked, and I forgot about it. Then I was poking at an allocation profile for something unrelated and saw a wall of tiny byte[] allocations coming out of that writer. The payloads I understood. The framing I did not. Those two little strings never changed, so why was the loop minting fresh arrays for them a few million times a second?

Here's the loop that did it:

for (int i = 0; i < Records; i++)
{
    buffer.Write(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("data: "));
    buffer.Write(payload);
    buffer.Write(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("\n\n"));
}

Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("data: ") does exactly what it says every single time: it allocates a brand-new six-byte array, fills it, hands it to Write, and then it's garbage. Same for the "\n\n". The string is a compile-time constant, the bytes can never differ between iterations, and I was still paying for a fresh array on every pass. Two constant tokens, two allocations per record, nothing to show for it afterward.

The literal that isn't a string

C# has a thing for this now, and it's been stable for a few language versions: the u8 suffix. Write "data: "u8 and you don't get a string, you get a ReadOnlySpan<byte> that points straight at a blob the compiler bakes into the assembly's data section. No encoding step at runtime. No array. Reading it is just handing out a view over bytes that were already there when the program loaded.

The one wrinkle is that a ReadOnlySpan<byte> is a ref struct, so you can't drop it in a field and keep it around. The idiom that gets you a name for it is a property:

static class Framing
{
    public static ReadOnlySpan<byte> Prefix => "data: "u8;
    public static ReadOnlySpan<byte> Suffix => "\n\n"u8;
}

Every read of Framing.Prefix returns a span over the same static bytes. Nothing is copied, nothing is allocated. The loop turns into this:

for (int i = 0; i < Records; i++)
{
    buffer.Write(Framing.Prefix);
    buffer.Write(payload);
    buffer.Write(Framing.Suffix);
}

Stream.Write already takes a ReadOnlySpan<byte>, so the span goes in with no detour through an array at all.

What it actually bought me

I measured it the way I measure most of this stuff: GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() around the work, best-of-five on a Stopwatch for the timing. I framed two million records each pass. The allocation number is the one I trust, because it's deterministic and doesn't wobble between runs the way milliseconds do.

GetBytes per write    best  109 ms    183.1 MB/pass   gen0=7   (checksum 54000000)
u8 literal            best   38 ms     61.0 MB/pass    gen0=2   (checksum 54000000)

The checksums match — same 54 million bytes come out either way, so this isn't a correctness trade. The framing arrays were 122 MB of garbage per pass, gone. Gen0 collections dropped from seven to two. And it ran about three times faster, though I'd lean on the allocation figure over the timing since the clock jumps around on a shared box.

Now the honest part, because 61 MB is not zero and I don't want to pretend it is. That leftover is the output buffer itself. I sized the MemoryStream to hold the whole batch, so there's one big array per pass by design, and that one's the real work. The u8 change didn't make the method allocation-free, it deleted the allocations that had no business existing: the four million throwaway arrays for eight constant bytes. The buffer you asked for stays. The garbage you didn't, leaves.

When I'd skip it

If you already hoist the encoded bytes into a static readonly byte[] once at startup, you've solved the per-call allocation too, and u8 only really buys you clarity and the guarantee that it's truly static data rather than a heap array someone could mutate. The place u8 earns its keep is exactly the trap I fell into: GetBytes on a string literal sitting inside a hot loop, where it looks harmless and quietly isn't.

And it only works for literals the compiler can see. The moment your bytes come from a runtime string (a header value, a user's name, anything built while the program runs), you're back to GetBytes, as you should be. u8 is for the constants: delimiters, protocol framing, fixed JSON keys you write to a Utf8JsonWriter, the "HTTP/1.1 " kind of thing. My honest opinion is that Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("some literal") should read as a small code smell at this point — if the argument is a quoted constant, there's almost always a u8 that does it for free.

Since I hit a snag pushing this one to the repo, here's the whole measured sample inline — a net10.0 console app, dotnet run -c Release and it prints the table above:

using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Text;

const int Records = 2_000_000;
byte[] payload = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("{\"id\":42,\"ok\":true}");

long WriteWithGetBytes()
{
    using var buffer = new MemoryStream(Records * 32);
    for (int i = 0; i < Records; i++)
    {
        buffer.Write(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("data: "));
        buffer.Write(payload);
        buffer.Write(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("\n\n"));
    }
    return buffer.Length;
}

long WriteWithU8()
{
    using var buffer = new MemoryStream(Records * 32);
    for (int i = 0; i < Records; i++)
    {
        buffer.Write(Framing.Prefix);
        buffer.Write(payload);
        buffer.Write(Framing.Suffix);
    }
    return buffer.Length;
}

long Measure(string name, Func<long> run, int reps)
{
    long checksum = run();            // warm up
    GC.Collect(); GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers(); GC.Collect();

    long bestMs = long.MaxValue;
    long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
    int g0 = GC.CollectionCount(0);
    for (int r = 0; r < reps; r++)
    {
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        checksum = run();
        sw.Stop();
        if (sw.ElapsedMilliseconds < bestMs) bestMs = sw.ElapsedMilliseconds;
    }
    double mb = (GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before) / (double)reps / (1024 * 1024);
    Console.WriteLine($"{name,-22} best {bestMs,4} ms {mb,7:F1} MB/pass gen0={GC.CollectionCount(0) - g0} (checksum {checksum})");
    return checksum;
}

Console.WriteLine($"Framing {Records:N0} records, best of 5 passes each\n");
long a = Measure("GetBytes per write", WriteWithGetBytes, 5);
long b = Measure("u8 literal", WriteWithU8, 5);
Console.WriteLine("\n" + (a == b ? "checksums match" : "MISMATCH"));

static class Framing
{
    public static ReadOnlySpan<byte> Prefix => "data: "u8;
    public static ReadOnlySpan<byte> Suffix => "\n\n"u8;
}

Anyone else have a GetBytes call hiding in a loop they forgot about? Go grep your hot paths for a quoted string argument — I bet you find one.

— still chasing allocations nobody asked me to chase

articles.title: AI found the vulnerability. Are we done yet?
articles.description: AI is finding serious vulnerabilities and writing increasingly capable code. PHP2Shell and Firefox show why proving, fixing and shipping those findings is still hard work.
articles.body_html:
What caught my attention about PHP2Shell was the PHP team's explanation of why fixing it took so long. A developer had noticed signs of the problem back in 2024. They had several possible fixes, but each came with problems: breaking compatibility, creating denial-of-service risks, or requiring changes to third-party extensions.

Imagine knowing there's a security problem in your code and having to choose which other problem you're willing to create to fix it. Now imagine that code is PHP.

AI helped researchers turn these flaws into working exploits. That's a big deal. But reading the maintainers' account, I kept coming back to everything they had to work through before they could ship a fix.

In October, PHP released emergency security updates for two critical vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell. They affect the PHP engine itself, and under the right conditions can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on a vulnerable server.

Finding a flaw, demonstrating an exploit, fixing the underlying problem and safely deploying that fix are different jobs. Being good at one doesn't automatically finish the others.

And before anyone puts off updating PHP because an exploit sounds difficult: please don't. Security researchers have demonstrated working attacks, and NVISO's October 28 update cited reports of targeted exploitation. Difficulty is not a security patch.

Ok, but the AI found it. Isn't that the hard part?

It's a hard part. And in this case the models helped with more than just finding the bugs.

According to Wiz, the flaws involve how PHP handles fatal errors, especially out-of-memory failures. An interrupted request can leave internal state partially initialized or pointing at freed memory. Later processing may reuse that invalid state, leading to memory disclosure or corruption.

The first signs of the out-of-memory problem appeared while a PHP developer was fixing an issue from a 2024 security audit. A possible exploit was theorized, but no concrete path to remote code execution had been established at the time.

The Foundation describes the stalled decision on a fix as a structural failure involving both the team's process and limited resources. Reports from Calif, OpenAI and Wiz in 2026 made the impact clearer, and the security team prioritized a fix across supported PHP versions.

Wiz says frontier models helped it develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours. Each target still required testing, debugging and adaptation to its memory layout.

Finding the crack is a start. The rest of the mechanism still matters.

The distinction mattered after disclosure too. In its October 28 guidance, NVISO cited a report of targeted compromise and a successful attack against a challenge server, with a public proof of concept. It had not observed successful exploitation in its own telemetry. There was no reliable universal public exploit at that point, and many non-functional tools were being circulated.

AWS identified attempted exploits against its honeypot before public disclosure, but couldn't tell whether they would have succeeded against real systems. When a model generates an exploit, I'd ask the same question: what shows that it actually works? Sending a payload or getting a convincing explanation isn't enough. We need to reproduce the result under realistic conditions.

What happened with Firefox?

Mozilla used a security analysis pipeline with Claude Mythos Preview and other models to investigate Firefox. Its engineers reported that Firefox 150 included fixes for 271 vulnerabilities identified with Mythos Preview. Their technical write-up describes findings across different browser components, including some involving sandbox escapes and bugs that had been around for years.

Some of those sandbox escape reports assume an attacker has already compromised a content process. Escaping the sandbox is a serious vulnerability, but a complete browser attack would also need a way to compromise that process first.

That's a lot of real bugs. Mozilla also says the improvement came from both more capable models and the work it put into the pipeline: steering the models, filtering reports and giving them a way to produce test cases. The pipeline was adapted to Firefox, with feedback from the engineers handling the reports.

Mozilla says more than 100 people contributed code to the effort, with others involved in triage, testing and releases. In an interview with TechCrunch, Mozilla's Brian Grinstead said that, for the bugs discussed there, an engineer wrote each patch and another reviewed it. The team also asked AI for suggested patches, but those generally weren't ready to deploy directly.

A finding still has to become a fix people can safely use.

What does a working fix actually prove?

With PHP, stopping one proof of concept wasn't enough. The fix had to address memory management and error handling across supported versions.

If the agent's patch stops the exploit, I still want to know: does it address the underlying failure across the affected paths? Does it introduce a different way to exhaust memory? Does it work on the supported versions without breaking extensions? Passing the test for one exploit isn't proof that we've fixed the whole problem.

What do the benchmarks tell us?

SecureVibeBench reconstructs 105 C/C++ implementation tasks from changes that introduced real vulnerabilities. The agents implement the original requirements, rather than patch an already identified bug. In the June 2026 version of the paper, the best tested combination, SWE-agent with Claude Sonnet 4.5, met both the functionality and security criteria on 23.8% of those tasks.

These were specific, difficult tasks using models from 2025, not the newer frontier systems in the PHP and Firefox examples above. The result doesn't tell us how those newer models would perform. What I find useful is the question the benchmark asks: did the change meet the functional requirement without introducing a security problem?

For PHP, a benchmark score won't tell us whether a proposed patch handles each affected configuration. For Firefox, it won't tell us whether a sandbox escape starts from an already compromised process. Those answers have to come from investigating the actual behavior and checking the evidence.

So what do we do with the findings?

I'd use AI to find the bug and help fix it. But if I can't explain why the patch works, I'm not ready to ship it.

articles.title: What it takes to prove binary search works
articles.description: I used Dafny to verify binary search, broke its termination, and compiled the working version to JavaScript.
articles.body_html:
In my previous article about Proof Driven Development, I wrote about using formal specifications to check whether code does what we agreed it should do. Microsoft Research's PDD Kit uses Verus for Rust, though, and most of my work is in JavaScript. So I was left with a question: what can I actually try without rewriting my whole application in Rust?

I ended up trying Dafny. With help from a coding agent, I wrote and verified a small binary search, deliberately broke it, and compiled the working version to JavaScript.

If you haven't heard of Dafny, it's an open-source programming language and verifier. You write code and describe what must be true before and after it runs. Dafny checks the code against those rules using a solver called Z3, and can compile it to languages including JavaScript.

dafny-lang / dafny

Dafny is a verification-aware programming language

Dafny

Dafny is a verification-ready programming language. As you type in your program, Dafny's verifier constantly looks over your shoulder, flags any errors, shows you counterexamples, and congratulates you when your code matches your specifications. When you're done, Dafny can compile your code to C#, Go, Python, Java, or JavaScript (more to come!), so it can integrate with your existing workflow.

Dafny will give you assurance that your code meets the specifications you write, while letting you write both code and specifications in the Dafny programming language itself. Since verification is an integral part of development, it will thus reduce the risk of costly late-stage bugs that are typically missed by testing.

Dafny has support for common programming concepts such as classes and trait inheritance, inductive datatypes that can have methods and are suitable for pattern matching, lazily unbounded datatypes, subset types e.g. for bounded integers…

View on GitHub

What is Z3?

Z3 is a solver: you give it logical constraints and it checks whether they can be satisfied. Dafny uses it to help check whether the code could violate the rules we wrote.

Why binary search?

If you don't know binary search, don't worry: the internet definitely doesn't have enough articles about it yet. I even wrote one of them a few years ago, including the most important requirement:

  • Your list must be sorted.
  • Your list must be sorted.
  • Your list must be sorted.

Still true! Binary search looks at the middle of a sorted collection, discards the half that can't contain the value, and repeats. That sounds simple until you have to decide what happens with an empty array, a missing value, duplicates, or a search range with one element left.

I wanted to see what it would take to check those cases without listing each input in a test. So I wrote down what a correct result should look like and asked Dafny to check the implementation against it.

What are we actually promising?

Here's the contract I used:

method BinarySearch(a: array<int>, key: int) returns (index: int)
  requires forall i, j ::
    0 <= i < j < a.Length ==> a[i] <= a[j]

  ensures index == -1 <==>
    forall k :: 0 <= k < a.Length ==> a[k] != key

  ensures index != -1 ==>
    0 <= index < a.Length && a[index] == key

requires is the condition the caller must satisfy: the array is sorted in ascending order. Equal values are allowed.

The first ensures says the result is -1 if and only if the value is absent. The second says that any other result must be a valid index containing the value. If there are duplicates, returning any matching index is fine; this contract doesn't ask for the first one.

In other words, there are two cases: if the value is missing, return -1; if it exists, return an index where it appears. Both clauses work together: the first describes when -1 is allowed, and the second checks that any other result points to the value.

The implementation needs an explanation too

Here is the complete method, including the loop invariants:

method BinarySearch(a: array<int>, key: int) returns (index: int)
  requires forall i, j ::
    0 <= i < j < a.Length ==> a[i] <= a[j]
  ensures index == -1 <==>
    forall k :: 0 <= k < a.Length ==> a[k] != key
  ensures index != -1 ==>
    0 <= index < a.Length && a[index] == key
{
  var low := 0;
  var high := a.Length;

  while low < high
    invariant 0 <= low <= high <= a.Length
    invariant forall k :: 0 <= k < low ==> a[k] < key
    invariant forall k :: high <= k < a.Length ==> key < a[k]
    decreases high - low
  {
    var mid := low + (high - low) / 2;

    if a[mid] < key {
      low := mid + 1;
    } else if key < a[mid] {
      high := mid;
    } else {
      return mid;
    }
  }

  return -1;
}

The search range is [low, high): it includes low, but not high. At the beginning, that's the whole array. At the end, when low == high, there's nothing left to search.

The invariants describe what must remain true throughout the loop. The first keeps the range inside the array. The other two say that everything before low is smaller than the key, and everything at or after high is larger. If we find the key, we return its index. If the range becomes empty, those two facts explain why the key can't be anywhere in the array.

decreases high - low is the termination argument. The verifier checks that the remaining range gets smaller on each iteration that continues the loop. Without that check, we could miss a search that gets stuck repeating the same step.

With Dafny 4.11.0, the verifier reported:

Dafny program verifier finished with 3 verified, 0 errors

Those three verified items are the verifier's reported count for the sample; they aren't a count of all the individual properties. The method's contract, bounds and termination are checked under its precondition. Dafny's guide goes into more detail on preconditions, postconditions and invariants.

Getting Started with Dafny: A Guide | Dafny Documentation

dafny.org

Let's break it

I changed one line:

- low := mid + 1;
+ low := mid;

The middle value is too small, so moving the lower bound to the middle might seem reasonable. But we already checked that position; we need to move past it.

Suppose we're looking for 6 and only 5 remains. low and mid are both 2, so setting low to mid leaves the range exactly where it was:

The next iteration checks 5 again, and the one after that does the same. With low := mid + 1, low becomes 3, the range is empty, and the search returns -1.

Dafny rejected the changed version:

Error: decreases expression might not decrease

Dafny program verifier finished with 2 verified, 1 error

The error doesn't spell out the one-element case, but it points us to the right place: the search range isn't guaranteed to shrink.

But I write JavaScript

Dafny can compile to JavaScript. I compiled this sample with dafny build --target js and ran the generated program with Node. For [1, 3, 5, 7, 9], it returned 3 for 7 and -1 for 4.

Installation Instructions | Dafny Documentation

dafny.org

The generated JavaScript uses bignumber.js for Dafny integers. It also includes generated runtime code, so this isn't the same experience as adding a type annotation to an existing JavaScript function. To call the generated method from an application, we need an integration layer that supplies values in the expected representation. I tried that separately with a small session-policy function; the generated sample needed an export added before a Node wrapper could call it.

And remember the first rule? The array must be sorted. Dafny checks that calls from verified Dafny code satisfy the requires clause; our sample's Main does. But the search method itself assumes its input is sorted, and the generated JavaScript doesn't automatically check an array supplied by a JavaScript caller. We need to establish that guarantee at the boundary or elsewhere in the application. Checking every element on every call takes linear time, which can outweigh the benefit of binary search.

We also need to check how the JavaScript adapter converts values. Dafny integers are mathematical integers; JavaScript Number values have their own limits.

The proof also doesn't establish that we picked the right behavior. If the product needs the first occurrence of a duplicate, our current contract allows a different matching index. Dafny can verify exactly what we asked for and still leave the product team asking why the result isn't the one they expected.

How is this different from TDD?

With TDD, I could start with a failing test for searching [5] for 6, then write the search until that test passes. That case would expose the broken low := mid update, although the test runner would need a timeout because the function gets stuck. I'd also add tests for an empty array, a value at either end, a missing value and duplicates.

Those tests check the inputs I chose. Dafny checks the method against the contract for all sorted integer arrays in its model, including the cases I didn't think to write down. It also checks that the loop makes progress, so I don't have to wait for a particular test to hang before finding that problem.

There's a tradeoff: I had to write the contract and loop invariants. If I forget to specify that the result should be the first matching index, Dafny won't invent that requirement for me. A test can miss the same requirement, but it's often easier to write and read a concrete example of what a user expects.

I'd still use tests around the generated JavaScript: they can check the adapter and real inputs from the application, which sit outside this proof. TDD would help me develop those behaviors one example at a time; Dafny gives me a way to check a general rule about the search itself.

What changes with AI?

Formal verification isn't new. What's changing for me is how practical it feels to try it. Learning a verification language, writing the specification and working out the loop invariants all take time. On top of building the feature, that can make verification a difficult sell.

Here, a coding agent helped write the Dafny example and work through the verification. That gave me something concrete to read and experiment with instead of starting from a blank file. I could change mid + 1 to mid, run the verifier again and see what happened. Getting to that point took less effort than learning the whole tool before trying a small example.

That doesn't mean I can accept whatever the agent writes. I still need to understand the contract well enough to notice that it allows any matching index, and check what happens when the code is called from JavaScript. But if AI can help with the mechanics and make these experiments cheaper, formal verification becomes something more of us can try on code where it would previously have been hard to justify the time.

articles.title: What does it mean to formally verify software?
articles.description: Formal verification checks software against precise properties. Here's how that works and why it matters when AI can write code faster than we can review it.
articles.body_html:
You ask an agent to implement a feature. It changes the code, adds tests, runs them and gives you a nice summary. Everything is green. Then you open the pull request and realize you still have to answer a question: how do I know this actually works?

The tests help. Reading the code helps. Asking another agent to review it can help too. But a passing test tells us what happened for the cases we ran, and a confident explanation is still an explanation. Neither automatically tells us what happens in all the cases we didn't think to check.

This is where formal verification gets interesting. Not because it's new, or because AI invented it, but because we're producing more code with tools that can also help us reason about it. Having a separate way to check some of the claims about that code sounds pretty useful.

So, what are we verifying?

Before anything else, what's correct?. Well, as any experienced software developer would say, it depends. On what? Well, on you, or your product. Correct can mean a lot of things to different people, so before verifying something, we have to be sure that the behavior we're verifying is the right one.

For that, let me introduce you to some terms:

  1. A specification makes the behavior we care about precise enough for a tool to reason about it.
  2. A property is a particular claim we want to check against that specification or the implementation.

For example: "a user without access to a document must not be allowed to delete it". That contains both: the specification and the property. Now that we have this clear, we can start to verify stuff.

Formal verification uses mathematical reasoning to check whether the thing we're examining satisfies those properties, within the model and assumptions used for the check. Sometimes that "thing" is a design; sometimes it's an implementation; sometimes is an Jira message you received at 3am... Anyways, NASA's introduction to formal methods gives a useful overview of the family of techniques behind this work.

shemesh.larc.nasa.gov

How does a verifier check that?

The verifier needs two things: something to check and a precise rule to check it against. How it does that depends on the tool. A model checker can look at the possible states in a model and how the system moves between them. A program verifier can use a theorem prover to reason about the code and its specification.

For a function, you can describe what must be true before it runs and what it should guarantee afterward. Those are a precondition and a postcondition. You can also describe an invariant: a property that should remain true as the system changes. The Dafny tutorial explains these with small examples.

Getting Started with Dafny: A Guide | Dafny Documentation

dafny.org

The verifier checks whether the rule holds for the behavior it's examining. Depending on the method, that might mean all the behaviors described by a model, or only a bounded set. If it finds a violation, it may show you a counterexample: an input or sequence of events that breaks the rule. That's useful because you get something specific to investigate.

But a failed verification doesn't always mean the code is wrong. Sometimes the tool can't establish the claim with the information it has, or can't complete the proof. You might need to give it more detail before it can tell you either way.

You don't have to verify an entire application to get value from this. A team can focus on a critical decision, algorithm or design where a mistake would be particularly expensive.

Wait, don't we already have tests?

We do, and if you have a decent testing coverage, then you should be proud. Take a medal (not really). Now, since we already have, what can we gain from Formal Verification? Formal verification reasons about properties over the behaviors covered by its model or proof. That can let us make a stronger claim about those properties than a handful of passing examples can.

But the proof has a boundary. If we've verified a function that makes a permission decision, we still need to know whether the rest of the application calls it when it should, and whether it gives the function the right information. A proof of the decision doesn't automatically establish either of those things. (This may sound very familiar to what a unit test is, but trust me, it's different... a bit).

NIST makes this point when discussing formal methods and testing: assumptions used in a proof may not hold when the specification is connected to the implementation and its dependencies. Tests can help us check those connections and exercise the actual application.

This is also why I'd be careful with “the software is verified.” Verified against what, and how much of it? Those questions are more useful than the label on its own.

Where does AI fit in?

Writing specifications and proofs takes work. The verifier needs precise statements, and some properties need more guidance before the tool can establish them. That's a different skill from writing the implementation, and it's one reason this isn't something most of us add to every pull request. Just imagine if 5 years ago you had a Jira task for a feature, and then a sub task for unit tests, and then a sub task for a formal verification of your work... Workflows defined by the utterly deranged.

But now, we have agents! An agent can help with parts of that work: discussing requirements, proposing a specification, writing an implementation and working through feedback from a verifier. The important part is that the verifier checks the formal claim according to its rules. We're not relying only on the agent telling us it got the answer right.

That's the idea that interested me in Proof Driven Development. The agent helps produce the work, and a verification tool checks it against an agreed specification. I also tried proving binary search with Dafny, which gave me a better appreciation for the amount of detail involved in checking one damn function.

But, as everything humans do, Formal Verification would be as good as the people that define what correct means. An agent can help you understand a codebase, identify possible issues and ask you questions for scenarios you hadn't thought (sometimes even for scenarios that are only possible in 1 out of 200M universes...). If your property definition never mentions a key detail, or how a special behavior should behave, a proof generated by an agent won't add it magically to your work. The code can follow the written rules perfectly, and the agent may have wrote the most beautiful proof your eyes have seen, but if you didn't know all the details...

Is this only for critical systems?

Formal methods are useful in critical systems, but the ideas aren't limited to them. In a 2015 paper on formal methods at AWS, the authors describe using a model checker on a DynamoDB design. It found a sequence of failures and recovery steps that could lead to data loss, after the team had already done extensive testing. So there is some value!

How Amazon Web Services uses formal methods - Amazon Science

amazon.science

Most of us aren't building DynamoDB. But we do write permission checks, payment flows and other logic where the consequences of a missed case can be significant. Those are places where making a property explicit—and deciding how strongly we need to check it—is worth the discussion.

I don't think every feature needs a formal proof. But as agents make code easier to produce, we need to start thinking about stronger ways to prove the output. We cannot humanly verify everything the agent does, we weren't able to verify everything when we wrote it either, that's why bugs exists and will continue to exist.

The point is: can we take this concept to help us write better software? That's on us.

articles.title: The Array Hiding in Every params Call
articles.description: A four-line display-name helper was quietly allocating an array on every call through params T[]. Switching to C# 13's params ReadOnlySpan<T> took it from 107 MB to zero, with the call sites unchanged.
articles.body_html:
I was reading a gen0 allocation profile for a service that does almost nothing interesting, and sitting near the top was a four-line helper I'd written months ago and never thought about again. It picks a display name: try the nickname, fall back to the full name, fall back to the email, fall back to "Anonymous". It allocates nothing of its own. Or so I assumed. It was handing the garbage collector an array on every single call, and I never passed it one.

Here's the helper, more or less as it was:

static string FirstNonEmpty(params string?[] parts)
{
    foreach (var p in parts)
        if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(p))
            return p;
    return "Anonymous";
}

And the call site, which runs once per request:

string name = FirstNonEmpty(user.Nickname, user.FullName, user.Email, "Anonymous");

That looks like I'm passing four strings. What I'm actually doing is asking the compiler to build a string?[4], drop those four references into it, and hand the array to the method. params T[] has worked that way since C# 1. Every call with inline arguments mints a fresh array, uses it for a few nanoseconds, and throws it away. The strings themselves already exist and get reused; the array is pure packaging.

Measuring the packaging

I don't trust my gut on allocation sizes, so I measured it with GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() around a tight loop rather than a stopwatch. Allocation counts are deterministic, so the number doesn't drift between runs the way milliseconds do. Two million calls, rotating through a few fake users so the branch isn't always the same:

.NET 10.0.15, 2,000,000 calls each

params string?[]                106.8 MB  gen0=0  (checksum 18000000)

107 MB of arrays to pick a name two million times. Each array is only about 56 bytes, but 56 bytes times two million is real, and in a service choosing a display name on every request it's a steady drip, not a one-off.

I want to be honest about one thing in that output: gen0=0. The collector hadn't fired during my measured window, because this box has a roomy ephemeral budget and 107 MB didn't fill it. So this isn't a GC-pauses horror story. The garbage is real, it just hadn't been swept yet. On a busy box with a tighter budget, that's exactly the kind of drip that turns into gen0 collections you actually feel.

The one-word fix

C# 13 added params collections, and the one I reach for is params ReadOnlySpan<T>. Change the parameter type and nothing else:

static string FirstNonEmpty(params ReadOnlySpan<string?> parts)
{
    foreach (var p in parts)
        if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(p))
            return p;
    return "Anonymous";
}
