The call site doesn't change at all. FirstNonEmpty(user.Nickname, user.FullName, user.Email, "Anonymous") compiles the same way it reads. But now the compiler stack-allocates the arguments instead of newing up an array, because the span doesn't escape the call. Same loop, same inputs, same checksum:

params ReadOnlySpan<string?>      0.0 MB  gen0=0  (checksum 18000000)

Zero. The strings are still there, the result is identical, and the packaging is gone. The timing moved too, though I trust it less than the allocation number. Best of five runs in the same cloud container, I care about the ratio and not the absolute milliseconds:

array  : 36 ms (best of 5)
span   : 8 ms (best of 5)

Most of that gap is the allocation work itself plus the collections the array version triggers across repeated runs. In a real service you'd never see a clean 4x, but you would see the arrays disappear, and that part is deterministic.

When I'd leave it alone

This isn't a reason to go sed your whole codebase. The win only shows up when the arguments are passed inline at the call site, so the compiler can see they don't escape. If your callers already have a List<string> or a string[] in hand and pass that, you were never allocating a throwaway array, and a ReadOnlySpan<T> overload buys you nothing there. It also does nothing for boxing: if the parameter is params ReadOnlySpan<object> and you pass ints, each int still boxes onto the heap, array or not. And on a path that runs a few hundred times a day, none of this matters and I wouldn't touch it.

My honest opinion: for a hot-path helper you control, params ReadOnlySpan<T> is close to free money, because the call sites don't change and the signature reads the same. For a public API, I'd think harder, since a span parameter can't be captured in an async method or a lambda, and that constraint leaks to your callers.

Here's the whole thing I ran, if you want to reproduce it:

using System.Diagnostics;

static string FirstNonEmptyArray(params string?[] parts)
{
    foreach (var p in parts)
        if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(p)) return p;
    return "Anonymous";
}

static string FirstNonEmptySpan(params ReadOnlySpan<string?> parts)
{
    foreach (var p in parts)
        if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(p)) return p;
    return "Anonymous";
}

const int N = 2_000_000;
string?[] nick = [null, "", "jpeg_enjoyer", null, "  "];
string?[] full = ["Dana Okoro", null, "Lee Park", "", "Mina Roy"];
string?[] mail = ["dana@x.io", "sam@x.io", "lee@x.io", "al@x.io", "mina@x.io"];

static long RunArray(string?[] a, string?[] b, string?[] c, int n)
{
    long sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    {
        int k = i % 5;
        sum += FirstNonEmptyArray(a[k], b[k], c[k], "Anonymous").Length;
    }
    return sum;
}

static long RunSpan(string?[] a, string?[] b, string?[] c, int n)
{
    long sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    {
        int k = i % 5;
        sum += FirstNonEmptySpan(a[k], b[k], c[k], "Anonymous").Length;
    }
    return sum;
}

RunArray(nick, full, mail, 10_000);   // warm up
RunSpan(nick, full, mail, 10_000);

long Measure(string label, Func<long> run)
{
    GC.Collect();
    GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
    GC.Collect();
    int g0 = GC.CollectionCount(0);
    long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
    long checksum = run();
    long bytes = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before;
    Console.WriteLine($"{label,-28} {bytes / 1024.0 / 1024.0,8:F1} MB  gen0={GC.CollectionCount(0) - g0}  (checksum {checksum})");
    return bytes;
}

Console.WriteLine($".NET {Environment.Version}, {N:N0} calls each\n");
Measure("params string?[]", () => RunArray(nick, full, mail, N));
Measure("params ReadOnlySpan<string?>", () => RunSpan(nick, full, mail, N));

Have you found one of these hiding in your own hot path, or is there a params call you'd never convert because the callers always hand it an array already? I'd like to hear which side you land on.

— still benchmarking helpers nobody asked me to profile

articles.title: Monuments of India, Part 2: Domes, Arches, Realistic Stone and Finer Details in three.js
articles.description: Last time, I proudly showed you 101 Indian monuments built entirely from code. This time I have to...
articles.body_html:
Last time, I proudly showed you 101 Indian monuments built entirely from code. This time I have to confess something: some of them were, let's say, enthusiastic approximations. That story is in I Built 101 Indian Monuments in the Browser Using Only Code.

Qutub Minar was wearing a cupola it never owned. The Taj Mahal had a lovely tomb but no actual garden. Dilwara had one temple where there should have been five. And a few of my buildings had a gorgeous front and, behind it, a back that looked like I'd lost interest halfway.

So I went on a fixing spree. Real doorways and guard niches on the forts. A proper charbagh for the Taj. Backs, sides and windows for the palaces. Towns that crowd around the temples like they've been there for centuries. Stone that catches the light, with veining, weathering and pietra dura. And yes, trees: the right trees. No more mango trees in the Thar Desert. Khejri and babul have been called in.

It is still 101 monuments in three.js, still pure code, and still not a single 3D model file downloaded. Come see what got more real, and help me spot what still looks like it's fibbing about its age.

Live: monuments-of-india-nu.vercel.app ·

Code: github.com/amananandrai/monuments-of-india

If the models or the code are useful to you, or you just like them, please give a star to the GitHub repo and help other people find the project.

TL;DR

  • The masses were already right. The joinery was not. Domes, screens, doors, backs of buildings and the ground around them got a second pass, monument by monument.
  • Shared parts for the family, detail files for the building. One dome, one jali, one gopuram for everyone, plus a file per monument for what only that monument has.
  • Everything is still code. Plain files and three.js, no build step, no model files, 650,000 triangles at most on a desktop and 300,000 on a phone.

In this post

  1. What changed since part 1
  2. How a part gets into a building
  3. Domes · Kiosks and turrets · Pillars and columns
  4. Arches, doors and windows · Eaves, battlements and bands
  5. Temple towers · Forts and monasteries
  6. When the shared kit is not the building
  7. What stands around the building
  8. Stone that catches the light
  9. How I checked the work, and what went wrong
  10. What I would still not claim · Add your own monument

What changed since part 1

This is the second pass, with the pictures from the component guides. The masses were already right. Up close, a dome was still a bare bulb, a screen was still a square grid, and the ground around a building was often the wrong trees or the wrong water. The work since then fills in the joinery, gives a few monuments pieces that only they have, and plants each site with what actually stands there.

Here is the short version, in the order I did it:

  • Real entrances. Forts got passages, guard niches and doors spiked against elephants. Temples got stepped doorways and porches. Mughal tombs got iwans and arcades.
  • A detail file for every monument, so a building has its own finer architecture and its own setting, not just a generic kit.
  • Photograph reviews. I compared the models with photographs in batches and fixed what disagreed: the Taj, Charminar, the Lotus Temple, the Hawa Mahal and many more.
  • Corrections. Qutub Minar lost the cupola it never had and gained Smith's Folly. The Taj Mahal got its full four-quarter charbagh. Dilwara got its other four temples.
  • Backs, sides and windows for palaces, mosques and tombs, so you can orbit them without finding a blank wall.
  • Towns and water around the temples at Kedarnath, Tirumala, Trimbak, Varanasi and Ujjain, plus the Old City round Charminar.
  • The right trees and the right water, per site.
  • Surfaces: photo textures with normal and roughness maps, calligraphy, pietra dura, carved reliefs and banded masonry.
  • Performance: monuments load when you open them, shadows follow the view, and phones get a lighter build.

Before and after

Same monument, same site, rendered by the same code: the left side is the repository before the second pass began, the right side is today.

Qutub Minar. The old tower wore a cupola it never owned. Now it tapers to its real top, and Smith's Folly, the Alai Darwaza, the cloister and Iltutmish's tomb stand around it, on grass with a path and trees.

Taj Mahal. The old tomb stood alone on a red plinth. Now it has its pishtaqs, calligraphy, chhatris and a charbagh garden to walk down.

Dilwara. One temple became the whole group of five, each in its own walled court, among trees.

Jaisalmer. A smooth sandstone mound with a ring wall became a fort at its real size on its Trikuta hill, with bastions, the road up to the gate and a town inside the walls.

Hawa Mahal. A flat stepped front with no depth became a screen of carved jharokhas, with the court and ranges behind it, the street in front and the building's sides finished.

The pictures below are the ones in components.md. node tools/shoot-components.mjs draws each shared part alone, in plain light. On the site the same part carries shadows, a photo texture and weathering. What each function takes, and which file it lives in, is in architecture.md and realism.md.

The site is still plain files and three.js, with no build step.

How a part gets into a building

Each monument has two files.

  • js/monuments/<name>.js builds the masses: plinth, walls, towers, roofs.
  • js/details/<name>.js adds the finer architecture and the setting, from addDetails(f, g).

f is the group the home view frames. g is the whole site, so a river or a town can sit outside the frame and not pull the camera back.

A few rules hold for every part:

  • Metres, y up. A part stands on y = 0 and faces +z unless its comment says otherwise.
  • The stone is passed in. M.marble, M.red, M.granite and the rest live in js/helpers.js. A one-off stone is mat('#hex', roughness).
  • Merge when the part is done. mergeByMaterial(group) leaves one mesh per material, so a facade of hundreds of small pieces is a handful of draw calls.
  • Two faces never share a plane. An overlay sits 2 to 5 cm off its wall. node check-flicker.mjs <id> from tools/ finds the ones that do not.

Placing a row of windows is a loop around the four faces:

// A window on each face, 11 m out from the centre, the sill 13.6 m up.
for (const a of FACES) {
  d.add(onFace(at(windowFrame(2, 4.2, M.cream, { shape: 'flat' }), 0, 13.6, 0), a, 11.01));
}

at moves a part. onFace turns that move onto a wall: angle 0 is the +z face, the next number is how far out, and a third number walks along the face. aroundCircle and alongFace do the same for a ring of brackets or a cornice. Hundreds of identical merlons or columns go through inst(), one geometry drawn many times.

Domes

A dome is rarely just a dome. The bulb springs from a drum through a moulded neck, and the finial that crowns it tells you the tradition: a Mughal spike, a temple pot, a crescent.
Onion dome: neck, lotus crown, finial Lotus dome: ribs, a cup of petals, a crescent

onionDome(r, m) is a lathe of the shared onion profile. From 1.5 m radius upward (4 m on a phone) it adds two more lathes that ride on the same group, so moving, scaling or ribbing the dome carries them along:

export function onionDome(r, m, {
  crown = r >= (detail.low ? 4 : 1.5),
  neck = r >= (detail.low ? 4 : 1.5),
} = {}) {
  const o = lathe(ONION.map(([a, b]) => [a * r, b * r]), m, 48);
  if (neck) o.add(lathe(DOME_NECK.map(([a, b]) => [a * r, b * r]), m, 32));
  if (crown) o.add(ribbed(lathe(DOME_CROWN.map(([a, b]) => [a * r, b * r]), m, 32), 16, 0.1));
  return o;
}

The neck is the moulding where the bulb springs from the drum. The crown is the inverted lotus, sixteen ribs pressed in by ribbed(), which is the mahapadma the finial rises from. { crown: false } or { neck: false } leaves one off where a monument models its own. The Taj does.

Around that sit the other turned shapes: hemi for a plain hemisphere, persianDome for a pointed double curve, lotusDome for an onion with shallow ribs sitting in a cup of petals, petalRing for the petals themselves, and finial, kalash and crescentFinial for whatever crowns it. A temple pot, a Mughal spike and a crescent are three different functions, because they are three different objects.

Kiosks and turrets

The chhatri, a small domed kiosk on columns, is the silhouette of Rajput and Mughal skylines. Take them off a roofline and it stops looking like India.
Chhatri Mughal chhatri Guldastas
Minaret Jharokha

chhatri(r, h, m, domeM) is the domed kiosk on eight columns that stands on Mughal and Rajput roofs. At full detail each column gets a moulded base and a spreading capital, the eave gets a drip edge, and the dome sits on a low drum. mughalChhatri is the richer one: arches between the columns, a sloping eave, a ribbed lotus dome, and an optional crescent.

guldasta is the Lucknow roof turret, a thin shaft under a tiny onion and a spike. minaret tapers, takes a list of balconies, and is capped by a chhatri. jharokha is the oriel on brackets, screened on three sides, under a roof that can be curved Bengal ('bangla'), domed, or flat. banglaRoof is that curve on its own, for pavilions as well as windows.

Pillars and columns

Classical, plain and Corinthian Carved temple pillar Cluster pillar
Yali pillar Column trim on bare shafts

These are different orders, so they are different functions.

  • column(r, h, m, { order }) in js/details/colonial.js is a classical column: plinth, base, tapering shaft, capital. order: 'corinthian' adds flutes and acanthus. entablature and corinthianCapital are what a colonnade carries above it.
  • carvedPillar is a temple pillar: square base, octagonal shaft with two carved bands, a cushion and a capital.
  • clusterPillar is the Vijayanagara pillar, a shaft ringed by slender colonnettes. yaliPillar carries a rearing yali and its rider. Both are sculpted rather than stacked from boxes.
  • columnTrim(list, m, { capM }) dresses a colonnade that was built as bare instanced shafts: a plinth and moulding under each, a necking ring and an abacus at the head. It is on Agra Fort's Diwan-i-Am, the Padmanabhaswamy corridor, Mahakaleshwar's colonnade and the Secretariat loggias at Rashtrapati Bhavan.
  • pilasters are the flat ones, proud of a wall by a few centimetres.

The trim matters because the cheap way to draw forty columns is one instanced cylinder. That reads as a row of poles. Bases and capitals are a second instanced pass, so the shafts stay cheap and the order comes back.

Arches, doors and windows

Arch and its ring Iwan Niche
Window with a jali Classical door Gothic window
Temple doorway

archWall cuts an opening through a wall. archRing is the moulded band around it. niche is a blind arch with a half-dome hood, deep enough to read as a recess. iwan, in js/details/mughal.js, is the great recessed arch of a gate or a tomb front, with its door. arcadeSkin cuts a wall into a row of arched cells, each a door, a screen or a room. mughalDoorway is the smaller pointed door onto a dim interior.

The traditions that are not Mughal have their own doors, because a fanlight is not a torana.

  • templeDoorway is a stepped frame, a hood, timber leaves standing open, a lamp in the sanctum, and guardians. doorLeaves can take spikes, the iron points set against war elephants. doorFrame is the nested carved bands of a post-and-lintel door. interior is the dim room seen through it. templePorch is the small open porch in front.
  • classicalDoor, porch and pediment are the colonial and Indo-Saracenic set. gothicDoor, gothicWindow and oculus are the pointed portal, the two-light window and the round window.
  • windowFrame(w, h, m, { shape, screen }) is a window in a stone surround. screen: jali(m) fills it.

The jali, from a grid to a lattice

A jali is a pierced stone screen. It lets air and light through while keeping a room private, and it is one of the most recognisable things in Mughal and Rajput architecture. It is also the part that used to be a square grid. It is now the octagon-and-diamond lattice of Mughal and Rajput screens, one function for the cut and the shading so they cannot drift apart. A 22 cm grid:

float sJaliHole(vec2 uv) {
  vec2 p = abs(fract(uv / 0.22) - 0.5);
  float oct = step(max(p.x, p.y), 0.34) * step(p.x + p.y, 0.47);
  float dia = step(1.0 - p.x - p.y, 0.13);
  return max(oct, dia);
}

Up close, when the holes are large enough on screen not to shimmer, the shader discards the opening. The stone around it still casts the shadow. Far away the lattice stays a shading pattern. Modelling every hole on 101 buildings was never going to fit the triangle budget: 650,000 on a desktop, 300,000 on a phone.

The same trick covers the ornament that should stay cheap: frieze for a band of rosettes, carved(m, kind) for 'script', 'calligraphy', 'pietra', 'reliefs' and 'tiles', plus rosette, medallion, sunburst and lettering for the roundels and the raised names. The pattern lives in the shader. The mesh stays a wall.

Eaves, battlements and bands

Chhajja on brackets Merlons Railing

chhajja is the deep sloping eave. chhajjaRing is the round version. bracketGeo is the corbel that carries an eave or a balcony, and placeAll drops one copy at every point in a list. merlons is a row of pointed battlements. On a fort, rampart and bastionCrowns add the parapet, a string course and arrow slits, for a long curtain wall and for round bastions.

railing and railingRing are posts with pierced screens between them. balustrade is the classical version. beltCourse runs a band around a rectangular building, mouldings stacks courses into a plinth or a cornice, dentils is the row of small blocks under that cornice, and panel is a sunk field that can be carved or inlaid. wallWithGaps is a compound wall with openings left for its gates.

Temple towers

Shikhara Nagara temple Dravida vimana
Gopuram Mandap Temple niche

nagaraTemple({ w, h, m, halls, … }) builds a North Indian temple in one call: sanctum, curved spire, and halls stepping out in front. That is why Somnath, in the first article, fits under 1 KB. shikhara is the spire alone, with nagaraProfile and kalingaProfile as two tapers. bhumijaRows sets miniature spires between the bands of a Bhumija tower.

dravidaVimana is the stepped tower over a South Indian sanctum. Each storey's edge carries miniature shrines: kuta at the corners, shala along the sides, laid out by haraRow. gopuram(w, d, h, tiers, seed) is the gate tower, tier on tier of painted stucco figures. The seed is why Meenakshi's towers are not copies of each other. mandap is a pillared hall under a stepped roof. storeyedHall stacks galleries. pidaRoof is the stepped pyramid of slabs on its own.

templeNiche(w, h, m, { figure }) puts an image in a niche. For a long row, idol is the cheap standing figure in relief. trabeateGate is a post-and-lintel gatehouse, with guardians or carved beasts. dwajasthambha is the gold flagstaff in front of the sanctum. grandStair is the broad flight between side walls, with a landing and guardians.
Grand stair Figure frieze Statue, urn, pinnacle

figure, guardian, statue and figureFrieze are the sculpted ones. The great statues, Patel, Bahubali, Thiruvalluvar and the Nageshwar Shiva, are each one continuous skin, grown from a signed distance field in js/sdf.js and meshed in the browser, so a limb grows out of a body the way it does in a carving.

The temples got the biggest structural rethink in this pass. Ram Mandir now has three storeys with cusped arches and a 32-step stair. Somnath's spire rises in seven storeys over a three-tier plinth and a broad stair. Mahakaleshwar has three storeys of shrines under its spire. The shared parts that made this cheap, grandStair, storeyedHall and the cusped arch, are now available to every temple.

Forts and monasteries

Fort gate Rampart and bastion Monks' houses
Dharma wheel and victory banner

fortGate is a gatehouse with a real passage, guard niches, and leaves spiked against elephants. towerDetail adds string courses and arrow slits to a round tower. slitRow is a row of slits along a wall.

A gate that is only an arch painted on a wall reads as scenery. A passage you could walk reads as a fort.

For the Himalayan monasteries, tibetanBlock is the whitewashed mass with dark windows under a maroon band. quarters dresses a list of those blocks as monks' houses: windows in black surrounds, doors, beam ends, earth roofs, prayer-flag poles. dharmaWheel is the gilded wheel between two deer over an assembly hall. gyaltsen is the victory banner at a roof corner, shabkhep the pleated awning over a window, parapetDiscs the gilded discs along a parapet. tibetanDoor and tibetanPortico are the painted door and the pillared porch.

The ground under a hill monastery comes from js/details/terrain.js: heightField shapes a surface from a height function, rock where it is steep, scrub or grass where it is not, and mountainRing sets a ring of mountains around a valley. That is how Tawang sits on its spur, Kailasa is cut out of a basalt escarpment, Ajanta sits in its horseshoe gorge, and Amber stands on its ridge with Jaigarh's wall above.

When the shared kit is not the building

Shared parts get a monument into the right family. They do not make the Taj the Taj. The detail file is where a photograph would disagree with a generic kit.

The Taj Mahal. Each face is a pishtaq: a deep pointed arch in a rectangular frame, roofed by a half-dome, with calligraphy in black marble and inlaid flowers in the spandrels. Smaller arched alcoves with pierced screens sit either side. The parapet carries leaf-shaped merlons, the drum a blind arcade, and the four roof chhatris have arches, an eave and a lotus cap. The minarets take three bracketed balconies. The dome's own lotus is modelled here, so the shared crown stays off. And around it all lies the charbagh, the four-quarter garden that the first version forgot.

Konark. The Sun Temple is a stone chariot, so the plinth is wrapped in friezes of elephants and daily life, above and below the wheels. The Jagamohana stands on carved mouldings, with an image in a niche either side of each doorway. At the steps of the Natamandira, lions rear over elephants. The horses are sculpted.

Hawa Mahal. Each jharokha of the screen projects on a pair of small carved brackets under the sill. The white lime bands along the storeys are carved. A lotus crowns each domed kiosk. Flowering bougainvillea sits at either end of the pavement. The lattice holes stay in the shader, so the stone is still solid and the screens still cast shadows. Behind the screen there is now a court, with ranges and ramps, so the building is no longer a facade with nothing behind it.

India Gate, Charminar, the Taj, the Gateway of India and the Old Parliament House carry the most of this layer: roundels, lettering, nested arches, bracketed balconies, jalis, eaves, merlons, lotus domes. The others take the carving of their own tradition. Base mouldings and image niches on the temples. Banded bastions and jharokhas on the forts. Stacked iwans and inlaid stars on the Mughal tombs. Capitals, balustrades and eaves on the colonial buildings.

What stands around the building

Everything that is not the monument comes from js/details/realism.js, with the animals in js/details/animals.js. A part takes a list of spots, [x, z] in metres. Variation comes from a seed, so a visit looks the same as the last one. copies() instances the shape and marks it as dressing, which the home view ignores when it frames the building. Fifty trees are a few draw calls.

Twenty-one kinds of tree, one planter

Broadleaf Wide Dry
Columns and conifers Palms Shrubs

trees(spots, { kind, seed, y, h }) plants every kind. One table, KINDS, holds the default height, the plain crown, the full crown, the leaf and the bark. An unknown kind throws, naming itself. Only the banyan drops aerial roots. Six silhouettes cover the twenty-one: a broadleaf, a wide broadleaf, a dry umbrella, a column, a tiered conifer, and the palm.

Where What stands there
Delhi's avenues Jamun
Bodh Gaya and Sarnath Peepal, the bodhi tree
Kashmir Chinar, pale, on a thick trunk
Ladakh, by the Indus Poplar and willow
Tawang and Rumtek Fir
Ajanta, and the forests Teak and sal
The south Tamarind
Konark and the Shore Temple Casuarina behind the palms
Jaisalmer, Chittorgarh, the dry ridges Khejri, dhok, babul, ber 
// Twelve jamun down each side of a path. The seed keeps this avenue the same on every visit.
g.add(trees(
  [...along(12, [-58, 14], [-58, 185]), ...along(12, [58, 14], [58, 185])],
  { kind: 'jamun', seed: 6 }
));

along is an avenue. scatter fills a rectangle and stays out of the building. around is a ring.

Every tree starts as a trunk and one crown. That is all a phone keeps. On a desktop, upgradeTrees() replants that monument's trees with a leaning trunk, limbs, and separate leaf clumps, smallest planting first, for as long as the model stays inside its triangle budget. Palms grow fronds with leaflets. Deodars grow drooping tiers. Six specimen trees become full trees. A forest of 160 usually stays plain. Each tree also takes one of three forms of its kind, so a row is not a row of clones.

shrubs has three readings. Plain is a clipped green bush. dry: true is the grey-green scrub of a dry hill. flowers: '#d0306f' is a dark bush with a smaller muted cap, bougainvillea or marigold, deliberately not a bush made entirely of bloom.

Lamps, flags, boats, towns

Lamps, bench, bollards ASI board Fountains
Prayer flags Tricolour and pennant Marigold garlands

lampPosts are fluted iron posts with a scrolled arm and a glass lantern, lit at night. asiBoard is the blue board on two posts. fountains rise and fall into a ring of foam. umbrellas are the cane and cloth shades on bamboo poles. prayerFlags run from point to point in the five colours. garland hangs marigold strands, orange and yellow. flag is a rippling pennant, saffron or the Nishan Sahib. tricolour is the national flag with the Ashoka Chakra.
Country boats Ferry launches Cargo ship
Houseboats Stalls Town houses

boats, launches, ships and houseboats take a water height, so a boat floats on its lake. stalls stand outside temple gates and in Laad Bazaar at Charminar. townHouses builds two to five storeys with windows, doors and shop signs. tanks is the share of flat roofs that carry a black water tank, 0.7 by default and 0.15 in the fort town at Jaisalmer. cityAround lines streets on every side of a rectangle and leaves the roads in keep open. At Puri, two rows of houses stand outside Jagannath's outer wall, and the Grand Road stays clear.

Towns are the change I like most. Kedarnath has its pilgrim town along the stone path. Tirumala has the temple town round its Mada streets. Varanasi's old city wraps the Kashi Vishwanath corridor, and Ujjain's old town sits beyond Mahakaleshwar. The Gateway of India has Elephanta ferry launches and ships at anchor.
Traffic on the two bridges that have it

traffic runs only on the Howrah Bridge and the Bandra–Worli Sea Link. There are no motor vehicles anywhere else, and no people at all, so the monument stays the subject.

Animals

Nandi Elephants Horse and lion
Deer Yaks and camels

nandi sits before a Shiva temple. elephant can be stone or bronze. rideElephant adds cloth and a howdah. lion is a gate guardian, and the Lion Capital. deer stand at Sarnath and Sikandra. yaks are in the mountains. camels wear saddle cloths in the Thar. horse, scaled down, is the ponies at Kedarnath. The larger animals are one continuous skin, heavier than the rest of the kit, and the slowest of them are meshed while the map sits idle.

Ground, water, and the shade at a wall's foot

The first scenery was generous, and often invented. Mango and coconut stood in the desert. Pools sat where the ground is grass. A lawn ended like a tile.

Water was put back where the site has it, and taken out where it had been added. The Tungabhadra runs north of Hampi's Vittala compound, palms on its bank. A stone-rimmed lotus pond lies south of the Mahabodhi railing. The Shahi Baoli stands east of the Bara Imambara, a walled stepwell through an arched gate. Ramappa's lake lies beyond the temple garden. India Gate lost the canals at its piers. Jallianwala Bagh's flame stands on the grass. Rameswaram's sea sits east of the temple, in the town. Maota Lake at Amber mirrors the fort.

Paths are flagstones. Courses are 70 cm deep, stones are 1.1 m long, every third course is half-length, and the courses shift so no joint runs straight through. Each stone has its own tone. Far off, the joints drop away and the floor stays slightly mottled.

float row = floor(uv.y / 0.7);
float wdt = mod(row, 3.0) < 0.5 ? 0.55 : 1.1;
float xo = uv.x + row * 0.37;

A wall meets the grass in shade, not in a hard line. When a monument is shown, it is drawn once from straight above into a 512×512 height map (groundShade in js/surface.js). Upward faces darken where that blur stands well above them. Trees are left out of the pass, because they already cast shadows. It runs on phones too.

Ceremonial lawns stay mown: India Gate, the Taj, Victoria, the National War Memorial, both Parliaments. Elsewhere, desktops get grass tufts under about 0.35 m, kept 4 m clear of the monument and off any path.

Close to a building, the camera casts a ray toward its target. If it has entered a solid it steps back out, and it keeps about 1.5 m off a wall in front of it. The home view frames the monument, not the lawns around it, and fifteen monuments open on the view of their best-known photograph: the Taj down its garden, the Red Fort's Lahori Gate, Meenakshi's south gopuram, Hawa Mahal's street front.

At night, floodlights and festival lights come on and stars fill the sky. Press the Night button on any monument to see it.

Stone that catches the light

The shader still paints joints, veins, brick courses, weathering and a slight tint per piece, from world position, so nothing has to be unwrapped. A one-metre block is the same size on the Qutub Minar as on the walls of Agra Fort. Over that, most stones carry a CC0 photograph from Poly Haven: marble, red and cream sandstone, granite, laterite, dark coursed blocks, fort rubble, plaster, lime, khondalite, concrete and weathered planks.
Marble Red sandstone Granite

Each set has a normal map and a roughness map beside the colour, packed by tools/pack-textures.py. On a desktop the shader projects them the same way as the colour, so the stone catches the light as a rough surface. Phones keep the colour map. A set is fetched the first time a monument that uses it is opened, not all of them at startup.

On top of the stone comes the ornament. The Taj gets black calligraphy bands round its pishtaqs. Itmad-ud-Daulah gets pietra dura over its walls, towers and pavilion. CSMT gets buff stone coursed with blue-grey basalt. Rani ki Vav gets sculpted panels on its side walls. All of it lives in the shader, so the mesh stays a wall.

Shadows follow the view. The shadow map used to cover a fixed box around the whole monument, so on a large site one texel was most of a metre. It now stays about three-quarters of the camera's distance from its target, changes in steps so the shadows do not crawl, and is redrawn only when a step is crossed. Desktops start at full sharpness and step down for that visit if the frame rate cannot hold.

On a phone, below 760 px wide, ambient occlusion and reflections are skipped. Trees stay plain, the ground has no tufts, towns and traffic are thinned, and the heavier carving waits. ?detail=high or ?detail=low on the address chooses.

How I checked the work, and what went wrong

Procedural models fail in a particular way: they look fine from the home view and wrong from two metres away. So most of the second pass was checking.

  • Photograph reviews. I went through the monuments in batches and compared each model with photographs of the real building. That is how the Taj, Charminar, the Lotus Temple, Mahabodhi and the Hawa Mahal got their fixes, and how a handful of near-misses were found and closed.
  • Full audits. After the photo reviews I went round the whole set again, in groups: views and land forms, mountains and towns, then framing, missing pieces and flicker.
  • Headless checks. The scripts in tools/ run in Node and Playwright and check triangle budgets, heights, filters, flicker and detail counts. They stop a regression from hiding in monument number 87.

Things that went wrong along the way, as I found them:

  • Flicker. Two faces on the same plane fight over the pixel. Windows, glazing and sea were all guilty. check-flicker.mjs finds them, and the rule is now that an overlay sits 2 to 5 cm off its wall.
  • A dark seam at the foot of sculpted hills, where the land met the ground.
  • A black reflection pixel on the Bandra–Worli Sea Link.
  • Eleven models that were too tall for their real heights, brought back within them.
  • Water and trees that were simply invented. The first scenery was generous. The mango orchard in the desert was the most photogenic of the lot.

I also made some deliberate cuts. The jali holes are not modelled, because 101 buildings of them would never fit the triangle budget. People are not in the scenes, and motor vehicles appear only on the two bridges that have traffic, so the monument stays the subject.

What I would still not claim

These are interpretations, not survey records. The goal is that someone who knows the building can see its plan, its material and its setting, and that someone who does not can tell a gopuram from a shikhara, and Konark from a generic temple.

The rule from the second pass is small. Repeated joinery lives in one shared part, which is why the pictures above are a catalogue and not 101 separate models. The thing that makes a monument itself lives in that monument's file. The tree and the water are the ones the site's own notes name. A new dome profile does not need a new texture unwrap. A new tree is one row in KINDS.

If you know a building well and see something wrong, I would like to hear it. Open an issue with a photograph or a source, and it becomes the next fix.

Add your own monument

Adding another monument is still one module and one card in js/data.js.

  1. Create js/monuments/<name>.js with the masses: plinth, walls, towers, roofs.
  2. Add its card to js/data.js: name, place, dates, style, material and a few facts.
  3. Optionally add js/details/<name>.js with addDetails(f, g) for the finer architecture and the setting. Reuse the shared parts first.
  4. Run the checks in tools/ (budgets, heights, flicker). See tools/README.md.

The code is MIT licensed, so you are free to use it, learn from it and build on it.

Try it

  • Explore: monuments-of-india-nu.vercel.app. Open #taj-mahal, then #konark-sun-temple, #hawa-mahal and #jaisalmer-fort.
  • The guides, with every part: components, architecture, the setting, how it is drawn.
  • If you found this helpful, or you like the project, star the repo on GitHub.

Which building still looks least like itself? Tell me in the comments. That is the next detail file.

The component pictures are rendered from the repo by tools/shoot-components.mjs. The project's code is MIT licensed, and so is three.js. Photo textures are CC0 from Poly Haven. Map data is public domain from Natural Earth.

articles.title: A black box is not redaction — and three other things I got wrong building local PDF tools
articles.description: Take any PDF. Draw a black rectangle over a line of text in a viewer that lets you annotate. Save it....
articles.body_html:
Take any PDF. Draw a black rectangle over a line of text in a viewer that lets you annotate. Save it. Open it again and drag-select across the rectangle.

The text comes back.

That is the entire reason I built a PDF tool site, and it is also the first thing I got wrong.

A black box is a drawing, not a deletion

An annotation is an object layered on top of the page content. The characters underneath are still there, in the content stream, encoded exactly as they were before you covered them up. Select-all still finds them. Copy still copies them. Any text extractor still returns them.

Actual redaction means the characters stop existing in the file. Not hidden, not covered, not rendered white-on-white — gone from the content stream, so that extraction returns nothing.

I built the redaction tool around that distinction, and then I made the checker report a number instead of a picture. Counting characters inside the marked areas turns out to be the only way to tell a real deletion from a good-looking one.

Three different zeros

This is the part that took me longest to get right, and it is the part most redaction tools skip.

If the checker says "0 characters inside the marked areas," that sentence can mean three completely different things:

  1. The text is gone. The page had a text layer, you marked it, and now extraction returns 0. This is the result you want, and the report calls it CLEARED.
  2. There was never a text layer. The page is a scan. Every pixel is an image; there are no characters to find in the first place. The tool reports NOTHING TO MEASURE, because the 0 is the absence of a measurement, not a clean result. A scanner output can look identical to a properly redacted page and mean the opposite thing — one has no text because it never did, the other has no text because you removed it.
  3. You drew the box on empty space. Same 0, same false comfort. The text you meant to remove is three lines down.

The first version of my checker merged all three into a single "0" with a green tick. That is a security product telling you what you want to hear. The current version reports the source page's character count next to the output's, so a scan and a clean redaction can never look the same.

There is a fourth result, and it is the ugly one: the marked page still hands back extractable text after processing. The report says so in plain words and tells you to treat the output like the original. It has happened in testing. I would rather the tool say that than round up to success.

What actually happens to the file

The redaction runs locally: the page is rendered to a canvas at 2× (about 144 DPI), the marked pages are rebuilt as JPEGs at quality 0.9, and the result is assembled into a new PDF. Pages you did not mark are copied through with their original text layer intact.

That has a consequence the tool states on the report rather than hides: a rebuilt page is an image, so everything on it stops being selectable — including the text that was not inside a box. If you need the rest of the page to stay searchable, you cannot have that and a destroyed text layer on the same page. Pick which one matters for this document.

The leak nobody looks at

Redaction is about what is visible. Metadata is about what is attached.

I stripped Title, Author, Subject and friends, and the file still carried the old title. The cause: pdf-lib removes the catalog's reference to the XMP packet, but the packet itself survives as an unreferenced indirect object inside the document. Delete the pointer and the body stays.

The second mistake was the check. I searched the output bytes for x:xmpmeta and found nothing, so I called it clean. The object was compressed. A byte search over a deflated stream tells you nothing at all — and this is exactly the kind of false pass that makes a verification step worse than no verification step.

The fix was to enumerate every indirect object after stripping, decompress each stream (UTF-8 first, then deflate, then raw deflate), and count the ones that still contain an XMP packet. Streams over 5 MB are reported as unscanned rather than silently skipped, because "I did not check this" and "this is clean" are different answers.

On my test file: 1,634 bytes in, 766 out, no XMP left. Compressed variant: 1,256 to 754.

Two more surprises, both about what tools quietly drop

Rebuilding a PDF is a destructive operation and the destructive part is not always where you expect.

PDFDocument.create() plus copyPages does not carry Author, Title or XMP into the new document — so a merge tool built this way produces a file with the contents of both inputs and the metadata of neither. It also stamps its own Producer and Creator as pdf-lib (...). If you were merging to preserve a document's provenance, you did not.

Same for splitting: each part is a fresh document, so each part arrives with no author and no title, whatever the original had. A tool page claiming otherwise is a page contradicting its own code.

The page-level limits are equally unglamorous: splitting one page per file caps at 50 pages, converting to JPG caps at 100, redaction caps at 50, and every tool caps the upload at 100 MB. These are browser limits, not policy — past that point memory pressure starts killing tabs, and a tool that crashes halfway is worse than one that refuses up front.

How to check that nothing is uploaded

This is the claim everything else rests on, so it should be falsifiable in ten seconds rather than taken on trust.

Open the tool, open the browser's Network tab, and drop a file in. You will see no request carrying your document. What you will see is static assets, and Cloudflare's analytics beacon, which the host injects into every page it serves — that is the CDN counting visits, not your file going anywhere. Clear the log, process the file, and watch it stay empty.

Five tools, all of them local

Everything above is implemented in the browser with pdf-lib and pdf.js. No server, no queue, no upload step, because there is nothing to upload to.

  • Redact a PDF without uploading it — draw boxes, rebuild the marked pages as images, get a report that separates the three zeros. Not a certification, not legal advice, and not a substitute for a compliance workflow that requires one.
  • Strip metadata from a PDF — Info dictionary and XMP, verified by decompressing every object rather than trusting the pointer deletion.
  • Merge PDFs in the browser — page contents carried, metadata deliberately not.
  • Split a PDF into single pages — one file per page or fixed ranges, zero-padded names so part10 sorts after part9 and not before part2.
  • Convert PDF pages to JPG — 144 or 216 DPI, quality 0.92 fixed, one download per page or a single ZIP.

Disclosure: these are my own tools. No affiliate links, nothing paid, no account required.

If you need redaction that survives opposing counsel, this is not that product, and I would rather say so here than in a support email. What it is: a local check you can run before you send a file you are not sure about.

articles.title: What the Sentry SDK drops after a 429 quota response
articles.description: I'm building an error tracker, and I needed to know what an official Sentry SDK does when my ingest...
articles.body_html:
I'm building an error tracker, and I needed to know what an official Sentry SDK does when my ingest answers "you're over quota". I couldn't find anyone showing the wire, so I put a stub server in front of @sentry/node and logged every request it got.

The failure is silent. A Sentry issue from 2025 says users "struggle with “why isn’t it working”" until someone sends them to the Stats & Usage page. Nothing throws. Events just stop showing up.

Node v24.22.1, @sentry/node 11.11.0 (run-0-versions.txt), all local on 2026-11-09. The server is a 55-line stub I wrote, not Sentry. What Sentry's servers do comes from their public docs.

TL;DR

  • After one 429 with X-Sentry-Rate-Limits: 60:error:organization:usage_exceeded, I captured 10 errors and only 3 hit the wire: 2 accepted, 1 rejected. The other 7 never left the process. No queue, no retry, and one warn-level debug line.
  • The SDK backs off for exactly what the header says. With a 5s window it sent one probe every ~5s. A bare 429 with no headers blocked everything for 60s.
  • The SDK does report the loss in a client_report, but the report said 7 when 8 were lost, because it skips the event that got the 429. Under a bare 429 the report itself gets blocked: 11 local drops, none reported.

How the SDK handles a rate limit

It keeps a "disabled until" timestamp per data category, sets it from the response headers, and silently drops matching items before they hit the network until that time passes. There's no buffer of "send later" events.

That matches Sentry's rate limiting spec for SDKs: "Events, transactions, sessions, and/or any other supported payload type, depending on the communicated limits, are to be discarded during the period that the rate limit is in place." The billing side says the same in I've exhausted my quota, what now?: "When your quota is exceeded, events are dropped and cannot be queued or stored."

The parsing order in @sentry/core 11.11.0 (ratelimit.js). Rows 1, 3 and 4 are in my runs below; row 2 I only read in the source:

Response What the SDK blocks For how long
X-Sentry-Rate-Limits: 60:error:... only the listed categories (error) the first number, in seconds
X-Sentry-Rate-Limits: 60::... (empty category) everything the first number
429 + only Retry-After: 5 everything Retry-After
429 with neither header everything 60s

"Everything" includes the SDK's own client_report items. That matters later.

Step 1: a stub that plays "quota exceeded"

The stub accepts /api/<id>/envelope/, logs one JSON line per request, and answers 429 after CAP items of one category. Trimmed to the item loop and the cap decision:

// stub.js: fake Sentry ingest. Logs every envelope request to JSONL and can play "quota exceeded".
// Env: OUT (jsonl), CAT (error|transaction|span), CAP (items of CAT accepted before the cap),
//      HEADER (full|retry|none), WINDOW (seconds in the headers), RESET_MS (quota refills after this)
// ...
const typeToCat = { event: 'error', transaction: 'transaction', span: 'span', client_report: 'internal' };
// ...
    for (let i = 1; i < lines.length && lines[i]; i += 2) {
      const head = JSON.parse(lines[i]);
      items.push(head.type);
      if (head.type === 'client_report') report = JSON.parse(lines[i + 1]);
      if (head.type === 'event') items.message = JSON.parse(lines[i + 1]).exception?.values?.[0]?.value;
    }
    if (RESET_MS && cappedAt && Date.now() - cappedAt >= RESET_MS) { used = 0; cappedAt = 0; }
    const mine = items.filter(t => typeToCat[t] === CAT).length;
    let status = 200, headers = { 'content-type': 'application/json' };
    if (mine && used + mine > CAP) {
      status = 429;
      if (!cappedAt) cappedAt = Date.now();
      if (HEADER === 'full') {
        headers['x-sentry-rate-limits'] = `${WINDOW}:${CAT}:organization:usage_exceeded`;
        headers['retry-after'] = WINDOW;
      } else if (HEADER === 'retry') {
        headers['retry-after'] = WINDOW;
      }
    } else {
      used += mine;
    }

usage_exceeded is my own reason code; SDKs ignore it.

Step 2: an app that captures on a timer

The app captures boom #1, boom #2 and so on, then calls Sentry.close(3000) so pending sends and client reports flush. Trimmed to the init and the afterSendEvent hook, which prints what the transport got back for each error:

// app.js: capture N errors (and optionally a transaction each tick) and print what the SDK reports back.
// ...
Sentry.init({
  dsn: 'http://devkey@127.0.0.1:9999/1',
  debug: process.env.DEBUG === '1',
  tracesSampleRate: process.env.TX === '1' ? 1 : undefined,
  clientReportFlushInterval: Number(process.env.REPORT_MS || 60000),
});

// Detection hook: fires after every captured error, with the transport's response.
Sentry.getClient().on('afterSendEvent', (event, res) => {
  const msg = event.exception?.values?.[0]?.value;
  const verdict = res.statusCode === undefined ? 'NOT SENT' : res.statusCode;
  console.log(`${clock()} afterSendEvent ${msg} -> ${verdict}${res.headers?.['x-sentry-rate-limits'] ? ' limits=' + res.headers['x-sentry-rate-limits'] : ''}`);
});

Each scenario is one line in run-all.sh, which starts the stub and the app with the same env (after npm i --save-exact @sentry/node@11.11.0):

shot() { # $1 name, rest = env for both stub and app
  local name=$1; shift
  env OUT=stub-$name.jsonl "$@" node stub.js > /dev/null & local stub=$!; sleep 0.5
  { echo "## env: $*"; env "$@" node app.js 2>&1; sleep 0.3; echo "## stub saw:"; node summary.js stub-$name.jsonl; } > run-$name.txt
  kill $stub; wait $stub 2>/dev/null || true
}
# ...
shot 2-cap-60s       N=10 EVERY_MS=500 CAP=2 HEADER=full WINDOW=60

The baseline (run-1-baseline.txt, no cap) is boring in a good way: requests=5 error_events_on_wire=5 accepted=5.

What happens at the cap: 7 of 10 errors never leave the process

After the 429, the next errors are dropped locally. No wait, no retry, and the stub never sees them.

App side, from boom #2 to boom #5 (run-2-cap-60s.txt):

17:57:35.383 captured boom #2
17:57:35.387 afterSendEvent boom #2 -> 200
17:57:35.885 captured boom #3
17:57:35.888 afterSendEvent boom #3 -> 429 limits=60:error:organization:usage_exceeded
17:57:36.388 captured boom #4
17:57:36.388 afterSendEvent boom #4 -> NOT SENT
17:57:36.889 captured boom #5
17:57:36.890 afterSendEvent boom #5 -> NOT SENT

boom #6 to boom #10 look exactly like #4. The stub's view of the same run:

17:57:34.902 200 [event] boom #1
17:57:35.386 200 [event] boom #2
17:57:35.887 429 [event] boom #3 {"x-sentry-rate-limits":"60:error:organization:usage_exceeded","retry-after":"60"}
17:57:39.912 200 [client_report] discarded=[{"reason":"ratelimit_backoff","category":"error","quantity":7}]
requests=4 error_events_on_wire=3 accepted=2

10 captured. 2 stored. 1 rejected. 7 dropped in the SDK. boom #3 is never resent. And captureException kept handing back event ids the whole time (run-8-eventid.txt: boom #4 id=5bc619400e85411889c667014b50bbc1 for an event that never left).

With debug: true (run-2b-cap-debug.txt, 4 errors), these are the lines around the cap. The rest is 27 "Integration installed" lines and init noise:

Sentry Logger [warn]: Sentry responded with status code 429 to sent event.
17:57:41.978 afterSendEvent boom #3 -> 429 limits=60:error:organization:usage_exceeded
Sentry Logger [log]: Captured error event `boom #4`
17:57:42.477 captured boom #4
Sentry Logger [log]: Recording outcome: "ratelimit_backoff:error"
17:57:42.478 afterSendEvent boom #4 -> NOT SENT

One warn for the 429. Every drop after that is a log line. Keep only warnings and you see the first one and nothing else.

Category limits only block that category

A limit on span doesn't touch errors. The SDK keeps one timer per category, so errors kept flowing while spans were blocked. run-3-span-only.txt used CAT=span TX=1, so each tick sent one error and one span envelope:

17:57:45.100 200 [event] boom #3
17:57:45.600 429 [span] {"x-sentry-rate-limits":"60:span:organization:usage_exceeded","retry-after":"60"}
17:57:45.602 200 [event] boom #4
17:57:46.105 200 [event] boom #5
17:57:46.606 200 [event] boom #6
17:57:47.109 200 [client_report] discarded=[{"reason":"ratelimit_backoff","category":"span","quantity":3}]

Note the item type: with tracesSampleRate: 1, 11.11.0 sent span items, not transaction (stub-3-span-only.jsonl). If your proxy limits transaction, check what you actually receive.

How long it backs off, and when it tries again

It waits exactly the window it was given, then sends the next real event as a probe. If that one also gets a 429, the window starts over. With WINDOW=5 and one error per second (run-5a-window-5s.txt):

17:59:22.491 429 [event] boom #3 {"x-sentry-rate-limits":"5:error:organization:usage_exceeded","retry-after":"5"}
17:59:27.501 429 [event] boom #8 {"x-sentry-rate-limits":"5:error:organization:usage_exceeded","retry-after":"5"}
17:59:32.509 429 [event] boom #13 {"x-sentry-rate-limits":"5:error:organization:usage_exceeded","retry-after":"5"}

Under a still-exhausted quota you get one request per window, and that event is lost too. When the stub refilled the quota 6s after the cap (run-5b-refill.txt), events flowed again on the first probe:

17:59:42.635 429 [event] boom #8 {"x-sentry-rate-limits":"5:error:organization:usage_exceeded","retry-after":"5"}
17:59:47.644 200 [event] boom #13
17:59:48.645 200 [event] boom #14

boom #9 to #12 were dropped even though my stub would have taken them from about 17:59:43. The SDK can't know the quota is back until its window ends.

Without the rate-limit header, Retry-After: 5 gave the same 5s rhythm (run-4a-retry-only.txt). A bare 429 gave the spec's 60s default (run-4b-bare-429.txt):

17:58:11.283 429 [event] boom #3
17:59:11.330 429 [event] boom #15

The client report says 7. I lost 8

The SDK counts its drops and sends a client_report envelope. Raw line from stub-2-cap-60s.jsonl:

{"at":"17:57:39.912","ms":5717,"path":"/api/1/envelope/","items":["client_report"],"status":200,"client_report":{"timestamp":1794243459.91,"discarded_events":[{"reason":"ratelimit_backoff","category":"error","quantity":7}]}}

ratelimit_backoff comes from Sentry's client reports spec. Three things I only learned by running it:

  1. It doesn't count the rejected event. quantity: 7, but 8 errors were lost: boom #3 got the 429 and boom #4 to #10 were dropped locally. If you build an ingest, count your own 429s as well.
  2. It's on a timer. clientReportFlushInterval defaults to 60000 ms (from the SDK's type docs). Run 2 got its report at close(). With REPORT_MS=3000 (run-6-report-3s.txt) it came in batches: quantity 3, 3, then 1 at close. A process that dies hard before either never reports.
  3. An all-category limit eats it. With a bare 429, run-4b-bare-429.txt shows no client_report at all for 11 local drops. The debug run shows why (run-4c-bare-debug.txt): 
Sentry Logger [log]: Sending outcomes: [ { reason: 'ratelimit_backoff', category: 'error', quantity: 1 } ]
Sentry Logger [log]: Recording outcome: "ratelimit_backoff:internal"

The report is an internal item, and the spec says the "all" limit applies to internal too. So the report was blocked and counted as one more drop. run-4a-retry-only.txt only got its report because close() landed 5.007s after the last 429, just past the window.

How to detect it from your app and your ingest

In the app, the afterSendEvent hook from Step 2 is the detector. It fired for every captured error: statusCode: 429 for the rejected one, none for local drops. Swap my console.log for a counter or a console.warn.

I only tested rate limits. From the SDK source, a network error also comes back with no statusCode, so this lumps both together. Spans don't go through this hook.

If you run the ingest, sum client_report discards plus your own 429s per DSN. discards.js does that over the stub logs (run-7-detect.txt, first rows):

stub-2-cap-60s.jsonl       429s=1 reported_lost={"ratelimit_backoff:error":7}
stub-2b-cap-debug.jsonl    429s=1 reported_lost={"ratelimit_backoff:error":1}
stub-3-span-only.jsonl     429s=1 reported_lost={"ratelimit_backoff:span":3}
stub-4a-retry-only.jsonl   429s=2 reported_lost={"ratelimit_backoff:error":8}
stub-4b-bare-429.jsonl     429s=2 reported_lost={}

The last row is the trap. Two 429s, zero reported losses, 11 events actually dropped.

Failure checklist

  1. Watching for exceptions. Nothing throws at the cap, and captureException still returns an event id for an event that never leaves the process.
  2. Filtering out debug logs. One warn for the first 429, then only log-level "Recording outcome" lines.
  3. Expecting a retry. The event that got the 429 is gone, and so is everything captured during the window (7 of 10 in run 2).
  4. Trusting client reports for the full count. They skip the 429ed event, arrive on a 60s timer or at close(), and vanish under an all-category limit.
  5. Sending a bare 429 from your own proxy or ingest. It blocks every category for 60s, client reports included. Send X-Sentry-Rate-Limits with a category if you only mean errors.
  6. Limiting the wrong category in a proxy. 11.11.0 sent span items, not transaction. Check the item types on your wire.
  7. Skipping Sentry.close() in short jobs. Pending client reports flush there. No close, no report.

Run it yourself

The listings above are trimmed. The full lab is run-all.sh (30 lines) plus stub.js, app.js, eventid.js, summary.js and discards.js: 11 scenarios in about 2.5 minutes, mostly the 60s bare 429. A second full run in a fresh copy gave the same counts.

I'm building Epure, a small self-hosted error tracker (errors only) that accepts events from Sentry SDKs and runs as an app plus Postgres in Docker Compose (v0.x, Apache 2.0). This lab is how I'm deciding what my own 429 should look like. Nothing above depends on it. The tap method on its own is in Log what your Sentry SDK actually sends, and the flood side is in Your sampleRate won't save you from an error flood.

If you've hit a quota cap in production, how did you first find out events were being dropped?

articles.title: Lessons from building 30 small web tools in a week
articles.description: A week ago I needed a quick Base64 encoder for a token with emojis in it. The first online tool I...
articles.body_html:
A week ago I needed a quick Base64 encoder for a token with emojis in it. The first online tool I tried mangled the output. The second required signup. The third wanted my token uploaded to their server.

So I spent a weekend writing my own, then another six days adding every small tool I wished existed. Along the way I learned a lot about Web APIs that have genuinely improved in the last few years. Sharing what might be useful to other developers.

Why no framework

I know React or Vue would have made some things easier. But for thirty independent tools, server-rendered static HTML is honestly the right fit.

Zero JavaScript to load on first paint. Every page is independently cacheable at the edge. No build step means instant edits. No supply chain risk because there are zero npm packages to audit. And the tools work offline after the first page load.

Would hand-rolled vanilla JavaScript on static HTML beat Next.js for this use case? In my benchmarks, yes. Because there is nothing to hydrate. The browser receives HTML, parses a few hundred lines of CSS, then runs a small page-specific script. That is all.

Base64 and the UTF-8 problem

Most online Base64 encoders mangle emojis and non-Latin characters. The reason is that the built-in btoa function in browsers only accepts characters below code point 256. Anything above, like an emoji or an Urdu letter, throws an error.

The fix is to run the string through a UTF-8 encoder first, convert those bytes to a binary string, then Base64 it. Decoding reverses the process. Two short helpers and the problem is solved for every language and every emoji.

I spent an embarrassing amount of time learning this the hard way. If you are writing any text-handling code in the browser, reach for TextEncoder and TextDecoder first. They quietly fix half of JavaScript's historic string problems.

JSON Web Tokens are surprisingly simple to read

A JWT is three pieces of Base64 separated by dots. The first two pieces are JSON after decoding. The third is a signature, which is just bytes.

To read a token, you decode the first two pieces with Base64 and parse them as JSON. That is the entire decoding process. About ten lines of code.

Verifying the signature is a different story and requires the issuer's secret or public key. That is why any public online decoder should be clearly labeled as reading only, never verifying. Users should not paste real production tokens into anything they do not control.

The Web Crypto API is genuinely good now

For years, developers reached for npm packages for anything cryptographic. That is no longer necessary for most use cases.

SHA-1, SHA-256, and SHA-512 are all one-call operations through the browser's SubtleCrypto API. Both text and files can be hashed. Random bytes for UUIDs, tokens, or session IDs come straight from the operating system's secure random number generator through crypto.getRandomValues.

MD5 is the only common hash missing, because it was deprecated out of SubtleCrypto for security reasons. If you need it for file checksum compatibility, you will have to include a JavaScript implementation. Do not use MD5 for anything security-sensitive.

UUIDs without any library

The v4 UUID specification is about ten lines of code once you have access to a cryptographic random number generator. You pull sixteen random bytes, set a few specific bits to mark the version and variant, then format as hex with dashes. Done.

A library adds nothing except bytes to your page. The browser's built-in random source is the same quality that your operating system uses for its own secure code.

If you need time-sortable UUIDs, version seven is similar in structure but replaces the first few bytes with a millisecond timestamp. That version is becoming the default for new databases because random UUIDs fragment B-tree indexes.

Unix timestamps come in four flavors

Different systems return timestamps in seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, or nanoseconds. A pragmatic auto-detector looks at the digit count. Ten digits is seconds, thirteen is milliseconds, sixteen is microseconds, nineteen is nanoseconds. This heuristic covers almost every real-world case I have seen.

Not exhaustive, but pragmatic. The alternative is forcing users to pick the unit themselves, which they get wrong half the time.

Regex pitfalls are real

While building a regex tester, I rediscovered two classic footguns.

First, patterns with the global flag that can match an empty string will infinite-loop unless you manually advance the last-match position when the match has zero length. The regex engine happily keeps trying the same spot forever otherwise.

Second, greedy quantifiers in nested groups can cause catastrophic backtracking. A pattern like a+ inside parentheses with a plus after the group will explore an exponential number of combinations on a string of many a letters. The browser locks up. Users learn to avoid this the hard way.

Both are fixable once you know they exist. Neither is well documented in most regex tutorials.

The cookie consent banner is thirty lines

Most sites solve consent banners with a fifty-kilobyte third-party library. The entire concept is a div with two buttons, a localStorage key to remember the choice, and a link to the privacy policy. About thirty lines of vanilla JavaScript.

Writing this myself clarified what the regulations actually require: an informed choice stored per user, respected across the session. Nothing more. The third-party libraries ship a lot of code to handle edge cases most sites never hit.

Lessons from seven days

A few things that surprised me.

Writing eight hundred word explanations is harder than writing the tools themselves. A Base64 encoder is thirty lines. A good explainer page covering history, UTF-8 handling, URL-safe variants, and why it is not encryption is a thousand words. The content took longer than the code every single time.

Static HTML on a CDN beats any server setup for this workload. No build step. No hydration cost. No cold starts. Just HTML that renders instantly.

Lighthouse scores improve dramatically when you stop including frameworks you do not need. A page with only inline tool-specific JavaScript and shared CSS scores above ninety-five on performance without any optimization work.

The browser platform in 2026 is genuinely capable of replacing a surprising amount of server-side code for tool-style applications. The APIs are stable, well supported, and documented. If you are building anything that does not require persistent state, consider skipping the backend entirely.

Closing

Nothing here is new. All these APIs have been stable for years. But it was still useful for me to write them down after shipping, because the lessons are easy to forget.

If any of these observations save you an afternoon, I will consider the week well spent.

articles.title: Can You Render JSX on Windows Without a Browser? I Built an Engine to Find Out.
articles.description: Can You Render JSX on Windows Without a Browser? I Built an Engine to Find Out.   A while...
articles.body_html:
Can You Render JSX on Windows Without a Browser? I Built an Engine to Find Out.

A while ago, we shared an update mentioning that LeveloJS was rethinking its architectural foundation.

As the founder and lead developer of the project, I asked myself a question that felt unreasonable for a small setup:

Can we write regular JavaScript and JSX, yet render it directly onto an operating system window with zero Chromium, zero V8, and zero WebView?

I wasn’t interested in wrapping another browser inside an .exe. I wanted to find out what happens when you treat standard JSX as the direct blueprint for native, hardware-accelerated 2D graphics.

Today, I had one of those moments where I just sat back and stared at my monitor.

I ran the exact same JSX component on Google Chrome and inside the newly engineered LeveloJS Windows Native Host (levelo-windows).

I placed the two windows side by side.

The typography hierarchies (h1 through h6), the CSS Flexbox alignments, the dynamic button paddings, and the character measurements looked identical.

If you didn’t look at the title bar of the window, you honestly couldn't tell which one was the browser and which one was running directly on bare native pixels.

This Is Not an Official Release

Let me be completely transparent from the start: this is not a production release.

I haven't solved everything yet. Text input fields still need more platform wiring, complex scrolling is in the pipeline, and I still have edge-case node cleanups to refine.

This is an early engineering milestone. It is practical proof that our hypothesis—which felt like an impossible risk when we started—actually works.

Why I Refused the Existing Choices

When web developers want to target the desktop, they are usually forced into two paths:

  1. The WebView / Chromium Path (Electron, Tauri): You ship an entire browser or hook into the OS webview. It works, but your app inherits the massive complexity, startup lag, and memory footprint of a web browser.

  2. The New Vocabulary Path (React Native): You keep JSX, but you lose the web primitives you know. You cannot simply drop in a button, h1, or div—you have to relearn layout models around platform-specific components like View and Text.

I wanted a third path.

What if a developer could keep their familiar web-style primitives, but the engine underneath stripped away the browser entirely and spoke directly to the operating system?

What Is Actually Happening Under the Hood?

The architecture is broken into four distinct layers:

  1. QuickJS (The Embedded Runtime): Instead of pulling in hundreds of megabytes of V8 or Node.js runtime, I embedded QuickJS. It gives us standard ES2023 compliance, instant startup, and runs on a fraction of the memory.

  2. Zero-Copy OpCode Bridge: When a component updates, there is no Virtual DOM tree diffing. LeveloJS emits direct atomic operation codes (CreateElement, SetStyle, AppendChild) directly over a low-overhead FFI boundary into Rust.

  3. Taffy (The Layout Engine): Emulating browser layout by guessing coordinates is a trap. I wired the W3C Flexbox specification using Taffy. Every container, child, margin, and alignment calculation is solved natively by Rust according to true CSS standards.

  4. Skia (The Drawing Engine)*: Once Taffy computes the spatial bounds, pixels are blitted directly to the native OS window using Skia—the exact same high-performance 2D graphics engine that powers Google Chrome and Flutter.

Because the Web target and Native target are completely decoupled, a web application never loads or ships a single byte of native Rust binaries, and a native application never runs an embedded browser.

The Collaboration Behind the Journey

While I architected the core LeveloJS foundation, designed the CLI toolchain, and built the levelo-windows host from scratch, LeveloJS is also growing through collaboration.

My contributor, Joseph Nicholas Aburu—an experienced developer with over a decade of programming background—joined this journey to help explore what a truly multi-platform architecture can become. Having his insights and collaboration on optimization, ideas, and architecture reviews has been an invaluable asset in shaping the project's evolution.

Open source is built on shared passion, and LeveloJS reflects that spirit.

How I Actually Fixed the Rendering Parity

Getting rectangles to draw on a canvas is easy. Getting a native engine to match the nuanced typography, auto-sizing dynamic buttons, and hit-testing behavior of a modern web browser is brutal.

I spent weeks fighting alignment offsets, layout trees, and coordinate bugs. There were moments when my brain stopped working, the layout fell apart, and building my own engine felt like an overwhelming mistake.

It didn't magically fix itself. I had to tear down the rendering pipeline, isolate the Skia rendering logic from the layout calculations, and audit every single file step by step to trace where the coordinates were drifting.

By letting Taffy handle pure CSS Flexbox constraints and stripping away manual layout hacks from the Skia canvas layer, the pieces finally aligned through deliberate debugging:

  • Dynamic buttons began sizing and wrapping cleanly around their text content.
  • The Flexbox engine centered elements exactly where Chrome centered them.
  • Mouse events mapped directly to native event handlers, triggering real-time reactive state updates without lag.

I proved that you don't need a full browser engine just to render modern declarative UI.

What’s Next?

I am taking this step by step.

The next engineering priorities include:

  • Completing remaining tree-cleanup and lifecycle edge cases.
  • Expanding form controls and text inputs.
  • Researching the pipeline for Android and other platforms.

We don't claim to have all the answers, and we know there is a long road ahead. But building software is about having the courage to explore problems that others avoid.

I put my trust in Allah, we did the work, and the foundation is now alive and running.

LeveloJS is built and maintained under Motion Mind X.

Founder & Lead Architect: MD Saiful Alom Siam (@MotionMind2007)

Contributor: Joseph Nicholas Aburu (@Joseph4sure)

articles.description: A small sensor strapped near the shaft, a TV box rendering the shot, and a player who expects the...
articles.body_html:
A small sensor strapped near the shaft, a TV box rendering the shot, and a player who expects the ball to go where they aimed. Six months of that taught us that the hard part is never the fusion math — it is agreeing on what "zero" means.

Mounting beats math

The same firmware, the same swing, two different mounts: 11 degrees of error in club face. You can spend weeks improving a Kalman filter and lose to a bracket that shifts 2 mm under load.

What we ended up doing:

  • A hard mechanical key. The bracket has a flat reference face that seats against a flat on the sensor housing. If it only fits one way, it only reads one way.
  • Mount ID in the payload. Every report carries which bracket revision it came from, so field data can be bucketed instead of silently averaged together.
  • Re-zero on every session start, not on a button. Players will not press "calibrate". They will take a practice swing. Treat the first quiet second as the reference.

The gyro bias drift nobody warns you about

Cheap MEMS gyros have a bias that moves with temperature. A sensor that sat in a cold car reads a few degrees per second of phantom rotation until it warms up. At 100 mph of club head speed that is not noise, that is a wrong shot shape.

Our fix is unglamorous: estimate bias during the quiet window, then keep re-estimating any time the device reports "not moving" for more than a second. The state machine matters more than the filter.

Latency is a product feature

The gap between impact and the screen updating is what players judge the whole product by. Our budget: 120 ms sensor to render. That forces decisions:

  • Do the minimum viable integration on the sensor, ship raw-ish quaternions, and do the heavy work on the box.
  • Never block the render on persistence. Write the shot to storage after the animation starts.
  • Preload every asset the shot animation needs. A single network fetch in the hot path blows the budget.

What we stopped measuring

We removed several "nice" metrics because they were unstable across mounts and made the app feel random:

  • Swing plane angle — too sensitive to the bracket's roll. Replaced with a simpler face-to-path number that players can actually act on.
  • Tempo ratios — precise on a lab bench, jittery in a living room. Kept as a coarse band instead of a number.

The lesson generalizes: if a metric changes when you re-mount the sensor, it is a property of your fixture, not of the player.

articles.title: I built a tool that films websites being built, commit by commit
